rd-school-c9-social-b.ch4-climate.title: Climate
rd-school-c9-social-b.ch4-climate.subtitle: Why Mawsynram drowns while Jaisalmer thirsts — the science of India's monsoon

sections.md:
Every year around **1 June**, newspapers across India carry the same excited headline: *Monsoon hits Kerala!* Farmers in Punjab, fishers in Odisha, reservoir engineers in Maharashtra and cricket fans everywhere all watch the forecast. For about four months, a giant wind system will sweep across the country, bringing **about three-quarters of India's annual rain**.

No single word shapes Indian life — its farming, festivals, food and even its economy — as much as **monsoon**. In this chapter we ask: what controls India's climate? Why is it hot in May but cool in Shimla? Why does the rain sometimes pause for weeks?

First, two words:
- **Weather** — the state of the atmosphere over an area at any point of time (today's temperature, humidity, rain).
- **Climate** — the sum total of weather conditions and variations over a large area for a long period of time (more than **thirty years**).

The elements of weather and climate are the same: **temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity and precipitation**. India's climate is described as the **'monsoon' type**, which is found mainly in south and southeast Asia.

This read follows the chapter: climate variations within India → climatic controls → factors affecting India's climate → the mechanism of the monsoon → the seasons → distribution of rainfall → monsoon as a unifying bond.

check.q: How long a period of weather records is usually needed to describe climate?
check.why: Climate is the average and variation of weather over a long period, generally more than thirty years.

sections.md:
Though India has an overall unity in its general pattern, there are **perceptible regional variations** in climatic conditions. Look at temperature and rain:

**Temperature.** In summer, the mercury occasionally touches **50°C** in some parts of the Rajasthan desert, while it may be around **20°C in Pahalgam** in Jammu and Kashmir. On a winter night, the temperature at **Drass** in Ladakh may be as low as **minus 45°C**. **Thiruvananthapuram**, on the other hand, may have a temperature of 22°C. In the **Thar desert**, the day temperature may rise to 50°C and drop down to near **15°C the same night**. On the other hand, there is hardly any difference in day and night temperatures in the **Andaman and Nicobar islands or in Kerala**. Coastal places have small ranges — the sea moderates them.

**Precipitation** varies in form, type, amount and seasonal distribution. In the upper parts of the Himalayas, precipitation is mostly in the form of **snowfall**; elsewhere it is rain. Annual precipitation varies from over **400 cm in Meghalaya** to less than **10 cm in Ladakh and western Rajasthan**. Most parts of the country receive rainfall from **June to September**. But some parts like the **Tamil Nadu coast** get a large portion of their rain during **October and November**.

In general, coastal areas experience less contrast in temperature conditions. Seasonal contrasts are more in the interior of the country. There is a **decrease in rainfall generally from east to west in the Northern Plains**. These variations have given rise to a variety in lives of people — in terms of the food they eat, the clothes they wear and the kind of houses they live in. (Think of sloping roofs in Kerala and the Northeast, thick-walled flat-roofed houses in Rajasthan.)

check.q: Which part of India gets most of its rain in October and November?
check.why: The Tamil Nadu coast receives much of its rainfall from the retreating and northeast monsoon in October–November.

sections.md:
There are **six major controls** of the climate of any place:

1. **Latitude.** Due to the curvature of the Earth, the amount of solar energy received varies according to latitude. As a result, air temperature generally **decreases from the equator towards the poles**.
2. **Altitude.** As one goes from the surface of the Earth to higher altitudes, the atmosphere becomes **less dense** and temperature **decreases** (about 6.5°C per 1,000 m). The hills are therefore cooler during summers — that's why the British built hill stations.
3. **Pressure and wind system.** The pressure and wind system of any area depends on the latitude and altitude of the place. Thus it influences the temperature and rainfall pattern.
4. **Distance from the sea (continentality).** The sea exerts a **moderating influence** on climate. As the distance from the sea increases, its moderating influence decreases and people experience extreme weather conditions — very hot summers and very cold winters. Compare Mumbai with Delhi.
5. **Ocean currents.** Along with onshore winds, ocean currents affect the climate of coastal areas. Any coastal area with warm or cold currents flowing past it will be warmed or cooled if the winds are onshore.
6. **Relief.** High mountains act as **barriers** for cold or hot winds; they may also cause precipitation if they are high enough and lie in the path of rain-bearing winds. The **leeward side** of mountains remains relatively dry — the *rain shadow*.

check.q: Why are hill stations cooler in summer?
options: They are closer to the sea
Temperature decreases with altitude as air becomes less dense
check.why: Higher altitudes have thinner air that holds less heat, so temperature falls as you go up.

sections.md:
**Latitude.** The **Tropic of Cancer** passes through the middle of the country, from the Rann of Kachchh in the west to Mizoram in the east. Almost half of the country, lying south of the Tropic, belongs to the **tropical area**. All the remaining area, north of the Tropic, lies in the **sub-tropics**. Therefore, India's climate has characteristics of both tropical and sub-tropical climates.

**Altitude.** India has mountains to the north with an average height of about **6,000 metres**. India also has a vast coastal area where the maximum elevation is about 30 metres. The **Himalayas prevent the cold winds from Central Asia** from entering the subcontinent. It is because of these mountains that this subcontinent experiences comparatively milder winters than Central Asia.

**Pressure and winds.** The climate and associated weather conditions in India are governed by:
- pressure and surface winds;
- upper air circulation; and
- western cyclonic disturbances and tropical cyclones.

India lies in the region of **north-easterly winds**. These winds originate from the subtropical high-pressure belt of the northern hemisphere. They blow south, get deflected to the right due to the **Coriolis force**, and move towards the equatorial low-pressure area. Generally, these winds carry very little moisture as they originate and blow over land. Therefore, they bring little or no rain. Hence, India should have been an arid land — but it is not! Why?

The pressure and wind conditions over India are unique. **During winter**, there is a **high-pressure area north of the Himalayas**. Cold dry winds blow from this region to the low-pressure areas over the oceans to the south. **In summer**, a **low-pressure area develops over interior Asia, as well as over northwestern India**. This causes a complete **reversal of the direction of winds** during summer. Air moves from the high-pressure area over the southern Indian Ocean, in a south-easterly direction, crosses the equator, and turns right towards the low-pressure areas over the Indian subcontinent. These are known as the **Southwest Monsoon winds**. These winds blow over the warm oceans, gather moisture and bring widespread rainfall over the mainland of India.

**Upper air circulation.** In this region, upper air circulation is dominated by a **westerly flow**. An important component of this flow is the **jet stream**. These jet streams are located approximately over **27°–30° north latitude**; therefore, they are known as **subtropical westerly jet streams**. Over India, these jet streams blow **south of the Himalayas all through the year except in summer**. The **western cyclonic disturbances** experienced in the north and north-western parts of the country are brought in by this westerly flow — they give the winter rain so important for wheat. In summer, the subtropical westerly jet stream moves north of the Himalayas with the apparent movement of the sun. An **easterly jet stream**, called the tropical easterly jet stream, blows over **peninsular India, approximately over 14°N** during the summer months.

> *Coriolis force:* an apparent force caused by the Earth's rotation, which deflects winds to the **right in the northern hemisphere** and to the left in the southern hemisphere. It is also called **Ferrel's Law**.
keyTerms: Coriolis force — deflection of winds by Earth's rotation (right in the north)
Jet stream — narrow belt of high-altitude (above 12,000 m) westerly winds, up to about 110 km/h in summer and 184 km/h in winter
Western cyclonic disturbances — winter weather systems from the Mediterranean
Southwest monsoon — moist summer winds from the Indian Ocean

check.q: What causes the complete reversal of winds in summer over India?
options: A high-pressure area over the Himalayas
A low-pressure area over interior Asia and northwest India
check.why: In summer intense heating creates low pressure over interior Asia and northwest India, drawing winds from the southern Indian Ocean as the southwest monsoon.

sections.md:
The climate of India is strongly influenced by monsoon winds. The sailors who came to India in historic times were one of the first to have noticed the phenomenon. They benefited from the reversal of the wind system as they came to India. The Arabs, who also came to India as traders, named this seasonal reversal of the wind system **'monsoon'** — from the Arabic word **mausim**, literally meaning **season**.

The monsoons are experienced in the **tropical area roughly between 20°N and 20°S**. To understand the mechanism of the monsoons, the following facts are important:

1. **Differential heating and cooling of land and water** creates low pressure on the landmass of India while the seas around experience comparatively high pressure.
2. The shift of the position of the **Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)** in summer over the **Ganga plain**. (This is the equatorial trough normally positioned about 5°N of the equator. It is also known as the **monsoon trough** during the monsoon season.)
3. The presence of the **high-pressure area east of Madagascar**, approximately at 20°S over the Indian Ocean. The intensity and position of this high-pressure area affects the Indian Monsoon.
4. The **Tibetan plateau gets intensely heated** during summer, which results in strong vertical air currents and the formation of low pressure over the plateau at about 9 km above sea level.
5. The movement of the **westerly jet stream to the north of the Himalayas** and the presence of the **tropical easterly jet stream** over the Indian peninsula during summer.

Apart from this, it has also been noticed that changes in the pressure conditions over the southern oceans also affect the monsoons. Normally when the tropical eastern South Pacific Ocean experiences high pressure, the tropical eastern Indian Ocean experiences low pressure. But in certain years, there is a reversal in the pressure conditions and the eastern Pacific has lower pressure in comparison to the eastern Indian Ocean. This periodic change in pressure conditions is known as the **Southern Oscillation (SO)**. The difference in pressure over Tahiti (Pacific Ocean, 18°S/149°W) and Darwin in northern Australia (Indian Ocean, 12°30'S/131°E) is computed to predict the intensity of the monsoons. If the pressure differences are negative, it would mean below-average and late monsoons. A feature connected with the SO is the **El Niño**, a warm ocean current that flows past the Peruvian coast in place of the cold Peruvian current every 2 to 5 years. The changes in pressure conditions are connected to El Niño; hence the phenomenon is referred to as **ENSO** (El Niño Southern Oscillation).

**Onset and withdrawal.** The **ITCZ** is a broad trough of low pressure in equatorial latitudes, where the northeast and the southeast trade winds converge. In July, the ITCZ is located around **20°N–25°N latitudes** (over the Gangetic plain). The southeast trades of the southern hemisphere cross the equator and start blowing from southwest to northeast due to the Coriolis force. These become the **southwest monsoons**. In winter, the ITCZ moves southward, and so the reversal of winds from northeast to south and southwest takes place — the **northeast monsoons**.

The monsoon arrives at the southern tip of the Indian peninsula generally by the **first week of June**. Subsequently, it proceeds into **two branches**: the **Arabian Sea branch** and the **Bay of Bengal branch**. The Arabian Sea branch reaches **Mumbai about ten days later, on approximately 10 June**. This is a fairly rapid advance. The Bay of Bengal branch also advances rapidly and arrives in **Assam in the first week of June**. The lofty mountains cause the monsoon winds to deflect towards the west over the Ganga plains. By **mid-June** the Arabian Sea branch arrives over Saurashtra-Kachchh and the central part of the country. The two branches **merge over the northwestern part of the Ganga plains**. **Delhi** generally receives the monsoon showers from the Bay of Bengal branch by the **end of June** (tentative date 29 June). By the first week of July, western Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana and eastern Rajasthan experience the monsoon. By **mid-July**, the monsoon reaches **Himachal Pradesh** and the rest of the country.

**Withdrawal** is a more gradual process. It begins in northwestern states of India by early **September**. By **mid-October**, it withdraws completely from the northern half of the peninsula. The withdrawal from the southern half of the peninsula is fairly rapid. By **early December**, the monsoon has withdrawn from the rest of the country.

The monsoon has a tendency to have **'breaks'** in rainfall; it has wet and dry spells. The monsoon rains take place only for a few days at a time, interspersed with rainless intervals. These breaks are related to the movement of the monsoon trough. When the axis of the trough lies over the plains, rainfall is good. When the axis shifts closer to the Himalayas, there are longer dry spells in the plains and widespread rain in the mountainous catchment areas of Himalayan rivers — floods follow in the plains.

check.q: Which branch of the monsoon gives Delhi its first rain, usually by the end of June?
check.why: Delhi generally receives the monsoon from the Bay of Bengal branch, deflected westward along the Ganga plains by the Himalayas.

sections.md:
The monsoon type of climate is characterised by a distinct seasonal pattern. Four main seasons are identified in India.

**1. The cold weather season (winter)** — begins from **mid-November** in northern India and stays till **February**. **December and January are the coldest months** in northern India. The temperature decreases from south to the north. The average temperature of Chennai on the eastern coast is between 24°–25°C, while in the northern plains it ranges between 10°C and 15°C. Days are warm and nights are cold. **Frost** is common in the north and the higher slopes of the Himalayas experience snowfall. During this season, the **northeast trade winds** prevail over the country. They blow from land to sea and hence, for most of the country, it is a **dry season**. Some amount of rainfall occurs on the **Tamil Nadu coast** from these winds as here they blow from sea to land. The weather is normally marked by clear sky, low temperatures and low humidity and feeble, variable winds. A characteristic feature is the inflow of **cyclonic disturbances from the west and the northwest** — low-pressure systems originating over the **Mediterranean Sea and western Asia**, moving into India along with the westerly flow. They cause the much-needed winter rains over the plains and snowfall in the mountains. Although the total amount of winter rainfall, locally known as **'mahawat'**, is small, it is of immense importance for the cultivation of **'rabi' crops**. The peninsular region does not have a well-defined cold season.

**2. The hot weather season (summer)** — due to the apparent northward movement of the sun, the global heat belt shifts northward. Hence, from **March to May**, it is hot weather season in India. In March, the highest temperature is about 38°C, recorded on the Deccan plateau. In April, temperatures in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh are around 42°C. In **May, 45°C is common in the northwestern parts** of the country. In peninsular India, temperatures remain lower due to the moderating influence of the oceans. The summer months experience rising temperature and falling air pressure in the northern part of the country. Towards the end of May, an elongated low-pressure area develops in the region extending from the Thar desert in the northwest to Patna and Chotanagpur plateau in the east and southeast. A striking feature of the hot weather season is the **'loo'** — strong, gusty, hot, dry winds blowing during the day over the north and northwestern India. Sometimes they even continue until late in the evening. Direct exposure to these winds may even prove to be fatal. **Dust storms** are very common during May in northern India. These storms bring temporary relief as they lower the temperature and may bring light rain and a cool breeze. This is also the season for localised thunderstorms associated with violent winds, torrential downpours, often accompanied by hail. In West Bengal these storms are known as **'Kaal Baisakhi'**. Towards the close of summer, there are **pre-monsoon showers** common in Kerala and Karnataka. They help in the early ripening of mangoes and are often referred to as **'mango showers'**.

**3. Advancing monsoon (the rainy season)** — by the beginning of **June**, the low-pressure condition over the northern plains intensifies. It attracts the trade winds of the southern hemisphere. These southeast trade winds originate over the warm subtropical areas of the southern oceans. They cross the equator and blow in a southwesterly direction entering the Indian peninsula as the southwest monsoon. As these winds blow over warm oceans, they bring abundant moisture to the subcontinent. These winds are strong and blow at an average velocity of 30 km per hour. With the exception of the extreme northwest, the monsoon winds cover the country in about a month and a half. The inflow of the southwest monsoon into India brings about a total change in the weather. Early in the season, the **windward side of the Western Ghats** receives very heavy rainfall, more than 250 cm. The **Deccan Plateau and parts of Madhya Pradesh** also receive some amount of rain in spite of lying in the **rain shadow area**. The maximum rainfall of this season is received in the northeastern parts of the country. **Mawsynram** in the southern ranges of the Khasi Hills receives the **highest average rainfall in the world**. Rainfall in the Ganga valley decreases from the east to the west. Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat get scanty rainfall.

**4. Retreating / post-monsoon season (the transition season)** — during **October–November**, with the apparent movement of the sun towards the south, the monsoon trough or the low-pressure trough over the northern plains becomes weaker. This is gradually replaced by a high-pressure system. The southwest monsoon winds weaken and start withdrawing gradually. By the beginning of October, the monsoon withdraws from the northern plains. The months of October–November form a period of transition from hot rainy season to dry winter conditions. The retreat of the monsoon is marked by clear skies and rise in temperature. While day temperatures are high, nights are cool and pleasant. The land is still moist. Owing to the conditions of high temperature and humidity, the weather becomes rather oppressive during the day. This is commonly known as **'October heat'**. In the second half of October, the mercury begins to fall rapidly in northern India. The low-pressure conditions over northwestern India get transferred to the Bay of Bengal by early November. This shift is associated with the occurrence of **cyclonic depressions**, which originate over the Andaman Sea. These cyclones generally cross the eastern coasts of India causing heavy and widespread rain. These tropical cyclones are often very destructive. The thickly populated deltas of the **Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri** are frequently struck by cyclones, which cause great damage to life and property. Sometimes these cyclones arrive at the coasts of Odisha, West Bengal and Bangladesh. The bulk of the rainfall of the **Coromandel coast** is derived from depressions and cyclones.

check.q: What are 'mango showers'?
options: Pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka that help mangoes ripen
check.why: Pre-monsoon showers at the end of summer in Kerala and Karnataka help in the early ripening of mangoes, so they are called mango showers.

sections.h: Distribution of rainfall and the monsoon as a unifying bond
sections.md:
**Distribution of rainfall.** Parts of the **western coast and northeastern India** receive over about **400 cm** of rainfall annually. However, it is less than **60 cm in western Rajasthan and adjoining parts of Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab**. Rainfall is equally low in the interior of the Deccan plateau, and east of the Sahyadris (Western Ghats). Why? Look at the rain shadow figure earlier. A third area of low precipitation is around **Leh in Jammu and Kashmir (Ladakh)**. The rest of the country receives moderate rainfall. Snowfall is restricted to the Himalayan region.

Owing to the nature of monsoons, the annual rainfall is **highly variable from year to year**. Variability is high in the regions of low rainfall such as parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat and the leeward side of the Western Ghats. So while areas of high rainfall are liable to be affected by **floods**, areas of low rainfall are **drought-prone**.

| Rainfall | Regions |
|---|---|
| Over 200 cm | Western coast, Northeast (Meghalaya, Assam), parts of West Bengal |
| 100–200 cm | Eastern India, Odisha, eastern Madhya Pradesh, parts of the Ghats' slopes |
| 60–100 cm | Upper Ganga plain, interior Deccan, Gujarat |
| Below 60 cm | Western Rajasthan, Kachchh, Ladakh, rain-shadow Deccan |

**Monsoon as a unifying bond.** You know by now how the Himalayas protect the subcontinent from extremely cold winds from Central Asia. This enables northern India to have uniformly higher temperatures compared to other areas on the same latitudes. Similarly, the Peninsular plateau, under the influence of the sea from three sides, has moderate temperatures. Despite such moderating influences, there are great variations in the temperature conditions. Nevertheless, the unifying influence of the monsoon on the Indian subcontinent is quite perceptible.

The seasonal alteration of the wind systems and the associated weather conditions provide a rhythmic cycle of seasons. Even the uncertainties of rain and uneven distribution are very much typical of the monsoons. The Indian landscape, its animal and plant life, its entire agricultural calendar and the life of the people, including their festivities, revolve around this phenomenon. Year after year, people of India from north to south and from east to west eagerly await the arrival of the monsoon. These monsoon winds bind the whole country by providing water to set the agricultural activities in motion. The river valleys which carry this water also unite as a single river valley unit.

> *Think about it:* Onam, Pongal, Baisakhi, Bihu, Teej, Nuakhai — so many Indian festivals mark sowing or harvest times set by the monsoon's rhythm.

summary: Weather is the atmosphere's state at a given time; climate is the long-term (30+ years) average.
India has a monsoon-type climate with big regional variations in temperature and rainfall.
Drass can fall to −45°C; the Thar can reach 50°C by day; Kerala and the islands have small daily ranges.
Rainfall ranges from over 400 cm in Meghalaya to under 10 cm in Ladakh and western Rajasthan; it decreases east to west in the northern plains.
Six climatic controls: latitude, altitude, pressure and winds, distance from the sea, ocean currents, relief.
The Tropic of Cancer splits India into tropical and sub-tropical zones; the Himalayas block cold Central Asian winds.
Seasonal reversal of pressure creates winter NE winds and summer SW monsoon winds; the Coriolis force deflects winds.
The subtropical westerly jet stream brings western disturbances in winter; a tropical easterly jet blows over the peninsula in summer.
Monsoon mechanism: differential heating, ITCZ shift over the Ganga plain, high pressure east of Madagascar, heated Tibetan plateau, jet stream shifts; ENSO affects strength.
Monsoon onset: Kerala ~1 June; Mumbai ~10 June; Delhi ~end of June; whole country by mid-July; withdrawal Sept–Dec.
Breaks in the monsoon depend on the position of the monsoon trough.
Four seasons: cold weather (mahawat rain for rabi), hot weather (loo, Kaal Baisakhi, mango showers), advancing monsoon, retreating monsoon (October heat, cyclones).
Mawsynram gets the world's highest average rainfall; rain-shadow areas like the interior Deccan are dry.
Rainfall variability causes floods in wet areas and drought in dry ones.
The monsoon is a unifying bond — farming, festivals and life follow its rhythm.

rd-school-c9-social-b.ch5-natural-vegeta.title: Natural Vegetation and Wildlife
rd-school-c9-social-b.ch5-natural-vegeta.subtitle: From mangrove tigers to Himalayan snow leopards — India's living treasure and how we protect it

sections.md:
Walk from the sea to the snow in India and you pass through many worlds. Mangrove roots poke out of salty mud in the **Sundarbans**, where tigers swim. Dense, dripping rainforest climbs the **Western Ghats**, home of the lion-tailed macaque. Teak and sal shed their leaves in the dry months of **Madhya Pradesh**. Thorny babul and khejri survive in the **Thar**. Higher up the **Himalayas**, oak and deodar give way to silver fir, then rhododendron, then alpine meadows where the snow leopard hunts.

India is one of the **twelve mega-biodiversity countries** of the world. With about **47,000 plant species**, India occupies **tenth place in the world and fourth in Asia** in plant diversity. There are about **15,000 flowering plants** in India, which account for **6 per cent** of the world's total number of flowering plants. The country has many non-flowering plants as well, such as ferns, algae and fungi. India also has approximately **90,000 species of animals**, as well as a rich variety of fish in its fresh and marine waters.

**Natural vegetation** refers to a plant community that has grown naturally without human aid and has been left undisturbed by humans for a long time. This is termed **virgin vegetation**. Cultivated crops and fruits, orchards, form part of vegetation but not natural vegetation. Virgin vegetation which is purely Indian is known as **endemic or indigenous species**, but those which have come from outside India are termed **exotic plants**.

- **Flora** — plants of a particular region or period.
- **Fauna** — species of animals.

This read follows the chapter: factors affecting vegetation → types of vegetation → medicinal plants → wildlife → conservation.

check.q: What are 'exotic plants'?
options: Plants that came to India from outside
check.why: Endemic or indigenous species are native to India; plants introduced from outside India are called exotic plants.

sections.md:
The huge diversity in flora and fauna is due to the following factors:

**Relief**
- **Land.** Land affects the natural vegetation directly and indirectly. The nature of land influences the type of vegetation. The **fertile level** land is generally devoted to agriculture. The **undulating and rough terrains** are areas where grassland and woodlands develop and give shelter to a variety of wildlife.
- **Soil.** Soils also vary over space. Different types of soils provide the basis for different types of vegetation. The **sandy soils of the desert** support cactus and thorny bushes, while **wet, marshy, deltaic soils** support mangroves and deltaic vegetation. The hill slopes with some depth of soil have conical trees.

**Climate**
- **Temperature.** The character and extent of vegetation are mainly determined by temperature along with humidity in the air, precipitation and soil. On the slopes of the Himalayas and the hills of the Peninsula above the height of **915 metres**, the fall in temperature affects the types of vegetation and their growth, and changes it from tropical to subtropical, temperate and alpine vegetation.
- **Photoperiod (sunlight).** The variation in duration of sunlight at different places is due to differences in latitude, altitude, season and duration of the day. Due to longer duration of sunlight, trees grow faster in summer.
- **Precipitation.** In India almost the entire rainfall is brought in by the advancing southwest monsoon (June to September) and retreating northeast monsoons. Areas of **heavy rainfall have more dense vegetation** as compared to other areas of less rainfall.

| Temperature zone | Mean annual temp (°C) | Mean January temp (°C) | Vegetation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tropical | above 24 | above 18 | Tropical |
| Sub-tropical | 17 to 24 | 10 to 18 | Sub-tropical |
| Temperate | 7 to 17 | −1 to −10 | Temperate |
| Alpine | below 7 | below −1 | Alpine |

**Ecosystem.** All the plants and animals in an area are interdependent and interrelated to each other in their physical environment, thus forming an **ecosystem**. Human beings are also an integral part of the ecosystem. A very large ecosystem on land having distinct types of vegetation and animal life is called a **biome**. The biomes are identified on the basis of plants.

**Forests and people.** Forests are renewable resources and play a major role in enhancing the quality of the environment. They modify local climate, control soil erosion, regulate stream flow, support industries (timber, paper, lac, honey), provide livelihoods for many communities, offer recreation, and control wind force and temperature. They also give shelter to wildlife.
keyTerms: Natural (virgin) vegetation — plants grown without human help and left undisturbed
Flora — plants of a region
Fauna — animals of a region
Photoperiod — duration of sunlight
Ecosystem — interdependent community of living things and their environment
Biome — very large land ecosystem identified by its vegetation

check.q: Which soil supports mangroves?
check.why: Mangroves grow in wet, marshy, saline deltaic soils such as those of the Sundarbans.

sections.md:
The following major types of vegetation may be identified in our country.

**1. Tropical Evergreen Forests (Tropical Rainforests)**
- Restricted to **heavy rainfall areas of the Western Ghats** and the island groups of **Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar**, upper parts of **Assam** and the **Tamil Nadu coast**.
- Best developed in areas having more than **200 cm of rainfall** with a short dry season.
- Trees reach great heights, **up to 60 metres** or even above.
- Since the region is warm and wet throughout the year, it has a luxuriant vegetation of all kinds — trees, shrubs and creepers — giving it a **multilayered structure**.
- There is **no definite time for trees to shed their leaves**, so these forests appear green all year round.
- Commercially important trees: **ebony, mahogany, rosewood, rubber and cinchona**.
- Common animals: **elephants, monkeys, lemurs and deer**. One-horned rhinoceros are found in the jungles of Assam and West Bengal. Besides these, plenty of birds, bats, sloth, scorpions and snails are also found.

**2. Tropical Deciduous Forests (Monsoon Forests)**
- The **most widespread forests of India**.
- Spread over regions receiving rainfall between **200 cm and 70 cm**.
- Trees **shed their leaves for about six to eight weeks in dry summer**.
- On the basis of the availability of water, they are divided into **moist and dry deciduous**:
  - **Moist deciduous** (200–100 cm rainfall): found in the northeastern states along the foothills of the Himalayas, eastern slopes of the Western Ghats and Odisha. **Teak, bamboo, sal, shisham, sandalwood, khair, kusum, arjun and mulberry** are commercially important species.
  - **Dry deciduous** (100–70 cm rainfall): found in the rainier parts of the peninsular plateau and the plains of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. There are open stretches in which **teak, sal, peepal and neem** grow. A large part of this region has been cleared for cultivation and some parts are used for grazing.
- Common animals: **lion, tiger, pig, deer and elephant**. A huge variety of birds, lizards, snakes and tortoises are also found here.

**3. The Thorn Forests and Scrubs**
- In regions with **less than 70 cm of rainfall**, natural vegetation consists of thorny trees and bushes.
- Found in the **northwestern part of the country**, including semi-arid areas of **Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh and Haryana**.
- **Acacias, palms, euphorbias and cacti** are the main plant species. Trees are scattered and have **long roots penetrating deep into the soil** in order to get moisture. The stems are **succulent** to conserve water. Leaves are mostly **thick and small** to minimise evaporation. These forests give way to thorn forests and scrubs in arid areas.
- Common animals: **rats, mice, rabbits, fox, wolf, tiger, lion, wild ass, horses and camels**.

sections.h: Types of vegetation — 2: Montane and mangrove forests
sections.md:
**4. Montane Forests**
In mountainous areas, the decrease in temperature with increasing altitude leads to a corresponding change in natural vegetation. As such, there is a succession of natural vegetation belts in the same order as we see from the tropical to the tundra region.

| Altitude | Vegetation |
|---|---|
| 1,000–2,000 m | **Wet temperate** forests: evergreen broad-leaf trees such as **oaks and chestnuts** |
| 1,500–3,000 m | **Temperate** forests with **coniferous** trees: **pine, deodar, silver fir, spruce and cedar**. These cover mostly the southern slopes of the Himalayas, places having high altitude in southern and northeast India |
| Higher | **Temperate grasslands** are common |
| Above 3,600 m | **Alpine vegetation**: temperate forests and grasslands give way; **silver fir, junipers, pines and birches**. They get progressively stunted as they approach the snowline. Ultimately through shrubs and scrubs, they merge into the **alpine grasslands** — used extensively for grazing by nomadic tribes like the **Gujjars and the Bakarwals** |
| Highest | **Mosses and lichens** form part of **tundra** vegetation |

Common animals in these forests are **Kashmir stag, spotted deer, wild sheep, jack rabbit, Tibetan antelope, yak, snow leopard, squirrels, shaggy-horned wild ibex, bear and rare red panda, sheep and goats with thick hair**.

**5. Mangrove Forests**
The mangrove tidal forests are found in the areas of coasts influenced by **tides**. **Mud and silt** get accumulated on such coasts. Dense mangroves are the common varieties with **roots of the plants submerged under water**. The **deltas of the Ganga, Mahanadi, Krishna, Godavari and Kaveri** are covered by such vegetation. In the **Ganga–Brahmaputra delta**, **sundari trees** are found, which provide durable hard timber. **Palm, coconut, keora, agar** also grow in some parts of the delta.

**Royal Bengal Tiger** is the famous animal in these forests. Turtles, crocodiles, gharials and snakes are also found in these forests.

> *Did you know?* Mangroves act as natural sea walls. During the 2004 tsunami and many cyclones since, villages behind healthy mangrove belts in Tamil Nadu and Odisha suffered noticeably less damage.

check.why: Sundari trees, which gave the Sundarbans its name, grow in the mangrove delta and yield durable hard timber.

sections.md:
India is known for its herbs and spices from ancient times. Some **2,000 plants** have been described in **Ayurveda** and at least **500 are in regular use**. The **World Conservation Union's Red List** has named **352 medicinal plants** of which 52 are critically threatened and 49 endangered. The commonly used plants in India are:

| Plant | Traditional use |
|---|---|
| **Sarpagandha** | Used to treat blood pressure; found only in India |
| **Jamun** | Juice of ripe fruit used to prepare vinegar (carminative, diuretic, digestive); powder of seed used for controlling diabetes |
| **Arjun** | Fresh juice of leaves cures earache; also used to regulate blood pressure |
| **Babool** | Leaves used as a cure for eye sores; its gum used as a tonic |
| **Neem** | High antibiotic and antibacterial properties |
| **Tulsi** | Used to cure cough and cold |
| **Kachnar** | Used to cure asthma and ulcers; buds and roots good for digestive problems |

*(This is a geography lesson about traditional knowledge, not medical advice. Always consult a doctor before using any plant as medicine.)*

> *Think about it:* Why is it important to protect forest plants that we haven't even studied yet? Many modern medicines — like quinine from cinchona bark — began as forest plants used by local people.

check.q: Which medicinal plant is described as found only in India and used for blood pressure?
check.why: Sarpagandha, traditionally used to treat blood pressure, is a plant found only in India.

sections.md:
Like its flora, India is also rich in its fauna. It has approximately **90,000 animal species**. The country has about **2,000 species of birds** — they constitute **13 per cent** of the world's total. There are **2,546 species of fish**, which account for nearly **12 per cent** of the world's stock. India also shares between **5 and 8 per cent** of the world's amphibians, reptiles and mammals.

**Elephants** are the most majestic animals among the mammals. They are found in the hot wet forests of **Assam, Karnataka and Kerala**. **One-horned rhinoceroses** are other animals which live in swampy and marshy lands of **Assam and West Bengal**. Arid areas of the **Rann of Kachchh and the Thar Desert** are the habitat for **wild ass and camels** respectively. **Indian bison (gaur), nilgai (blue bull), chousingha (four-horned antelope), gazel** and different species of deer are some other animals found in India. It also has several species of monkeys.

India is the only country in the world that has **both tigers and lions**. The natural habitat of the **Indian lion is the Gir forest in Gujarat**. **Tigers** are found in the forests of Madhya Pradesh, the Sundarbans of West Bengal and the Himalayan region. **Leopards**, too, are members of the cat family; they are important among animals of prey.

The **Himalayas** harbour a hardy range of animals that survive in extreme cold. **Ladakh's freezing high altitudes** are home to **yak** — the shaggy-horned wild ox weighing around one tonne — the **Tibetan antelope, the bharal (blue sheep), wild sheep and the kiang (Tibetan wild ass)**. Furthermore, the **ibex, bear, snow leopard and very rare red panda** are found in certain pockets.

In the rivers, lakes and coastal areas, **turtles, crocodiles and gharials** are found. The last of these is the **only representative of a variety of crocodile found in the world today**.

Birds in India are colourful. **Peacocks, pheasants, ducks, parakeets, cranes and pigeons** are some of the birds inhabiting the forests and wetlands of the country.

**Why is wildlife in danger?** In the present times, about **1,300 plant species are endangered** and **20 species are extinct**. Quite a large number of animal species are also endangered and some have become extinct. The main causes of this major threat to nature are:
- **hunting by greedy hunters for commercial purposes**;
- **pollution** due to chemical and industrial waste, acid deposits;
- **introduction of alien species**;
- **reckless cutting of forests** to bring land under cultivation and inhabitation.

> *Did you know?* The **cheetah** was declared extinct in India in 1952. In 2022, cheetahs were brought from Namibia to **Kuno National Park** in Madhya Pradesh in an attempt to reintroduce them.

sections.md:
Every species has a role to play in the ecosystem. Hence, conservation is essential. To protect the flora and fauna of the country, the government has taken many steps:

1. **Biosphere reserves.** Eighteen biosphere reserves have been set up in the country to protect flora and fauna. Of these, **twelve** are now part of the **World Network of Biosphere Reserves** (UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere programme); older editions of the textbook said ten. Examples: **Sundarbans** (West Bengal), **Gulf of Mannar** (Tamil Nadu), **Nilgiri** (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka), **Nanda Devi** (Uttarakhand), **Nokrek** (Meghalaya), **Pachmarhi** (MP), **Similipal** (Odisha), **Achanakmar-Amarkantak** (Chhattisgarh/MP), **Great Nicobar**, **Agasthyamalai** (Kerala/Tamil Nadu).
2. **Financial and technical assistance** is provided to many **botanical gardens** by the government since **1992**.
3. **Project Tiger (1973), Project Rhino, Project Great Indian Bustard** and many other eco-developmental projects have been introduced.
4. **National parks, wildlife sanctuaries and zoological gardens** are set up to take care of natural heritage — India has over a hundred national parks and several hundred wildlife sanctuaries.

The **Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972** provides the legal backbone: it bans hunting of listed species and regulates trade in wildlife products.

**What can you do?**
- Avoid products made from animal parts (ivory, skins, shells).
- Support local efforts to protect sacred groves, wetlands and lakes.
- Report wildlife crime to authorities; take part in bird counts and tree-planting drives.
- Remember the ecosystem includes us — we depend on forests for clean air, water and climate stability.

> *A thought:* The **Bishnoi community** of Rajasthan has protected khejri trees and blackbucks for centuries; in 1730, Amrita Devi and many villagers of Khejarli are remembered for giving their lives to protect khejri trees — a story often linked with the later Chipko movement.

Cheetahs reintroduced at Kuno National Park

fig.caption: Milestones in India's conservation story.

check.q: When was Project Tiger launched?
check.why: Project Tiger was launched in 1973 to protect India's tigers and their habitat.

sections.h: Map work, migratory birds and a field activity
sections.md:
**Map work.** The exercises ask you to show on an outline map of India: (a) the areas of **tropical evergreen forests** (Western Ghats, Andaman & Nicobar, upper Assam), (b) **tropical deciduous forests** (the large central and eastern belt), (c) **thorn forests** (northwest — Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana), (d) **montane forests** (Himalayas, Nilgiris), (e) **mangroves** (east-coast deltas and the Sundarbans). Then mark the **biosphere reserves** listed above. Colour each forest type differently and add a key — examiners check the key!

**Migratory birds.** Some of our most beautiful visitors come from far away. Every winter, birds such as the **Siberian crane, greater flamingo, pintail duck, curlew, common teal and many waders** fly thousands of kilometres from cold northern lands to Indian wetlands where water does not freeze and food is plentiful. **Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur)** in Rajasthan, the **Rann of Kachchh** (flamingo nesting grounds — 'flamingo city'), **Chilika lake** in Odisha and **Sultanpur** near Gurugram are famous for them. Draining or polluting a single wetland can break a migration route that took thousands of years to form.

**Field activity.** Make a **'species register'** for your school campus or colony over one month:
1. List every tree, shrub and bird you can identify (use a field guide or a free app with a teacher's help).
2. Note which are **native** (neem, peepal, banyan, jamun) and which are **exotic** (eucalyptus, gulmohar from Madagascar, lantana — an invasive weed from the Americas).
3. Record which birds come only in winter.
4. Suggest native trees for the next planting drive — they support far more local insects and birds.

> *Did you know?* The **Indian forest cover** is roughly one-fifth of the country's geographical area according to recent Forest Survey of India reports — below the one-third that the National Forest Policy has long recommended.

options: Indian wetlands stay unfrozen and have plenty of food

steps: 2,200 m lies in the 1,500–3,000 m belt
workedExamples.answer: Coniferous forest — pine, deodar, silver fir, spruce

summary: India is one of twelve mega-biodiversity countries with about 47,000 plant species (10th in the world, 4th in Asia) and about 90,000 animal species.
Natural (virgin) vegetation grows without human aid; endemic species are native, exotic species come from outside.
Relief (land, soil) and climate (temperature, photoperiod, precipitation) decide vegetation types.
An ecosystem is an interdependent community; a biome is a very large ecosystem identified by plants.
Tropical evergreen forests: >200 cm rain, trees up to 60 m, multilayered; ebony, mahogany, rosewood, rubber, cinchona.
Tropical deciduous forests: most widespread; 70–200 cm rain; moist (teak, sal, bamboo) and dry (teak, peepal, neem) types.
Thorn forests and scrubs: <70 cm rain; acacias, cacti, euphorbias; deep roots, succulent stems, small thick leaves.
Montane forests change with altitude: oak/chestnut, then conifers (pine, deodar, fir), alpine meadows, then mosses and lichens.
Mangrove forests grow in tidal deltas (Ganga, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri); sundari trees; Royal Bengal tiger.
Ayurveda describes about 2,000 plants; sarpagandha, jamun, arjun, babool, neem, tulsi, kachnar are common medicinal plants.
India has about 2,000 bird species (13% of the world) and 2,546 fish species (about 12%).
India has both tigers and lions; lions live in Gir; gharials are a unique crocodile species.
Threats: commercial hunting, pollution, alien species, reckless deforestation; about 1,300 plant species endangered.
Conservation: 18 biosphere reserves, botanical gardens, Project Tiger (1973), Project Rhino, national parks and sanctuaries, Wildlife Act 1972.
Migratory birds visit Indian wetlands in winter; protecting wetlands protects their routes.

rd-school-c9-social-b.ch6-population.title: Population
rd-school-c9-social-b.ch6-population.subtitle: 1.2 billion stories: how many we are, where we live, how we grow — and why people are the real resource

sections.md:
Imagine trying to count every single person in India — in high-rise flats in Mumbai, on boats on the Brahmaputra, in tents in Ladakh, on the pavements of Kolkata — within a few weeks. That is what happens in a **census**: an official enumeration of population done periodically. In India, the first census was taken in **1872**, and the first complete census in **1881**. Since then, censuses have been held regularly every **tenth year**. The Indian census is the most comprehensive source of demographic, social and economic data.

Why does a geography book care? Because **people are the most important element** of any region. They produce and consume resources and decide where cities grow and forests shrink. Population is the point of reference from which all other elements of social studies are observed: resources, calamities and disasters are meaningful only in relation to human beings.

We will study three big questions:
1. **Population size and distribution** — how many people, and where?
2. **Population growth and processes of change** — how fast, and why?
3. **Characteristics or qualities** — age composition, sex ratio, literacy, occupations, health.

Then we look at the **National Population Policy**.

(Numbers in this chapter are from the **2011 Census**, the latest full census used in your textbook. The census due in 2021 was postponed.)

check.q: When was the first complete census of India taken?
check.why: The first census was attempted in 1872, but the first complete census was carried out in 1881; since then it has been held every ten years.

sections.md:
Before the numbers, meet the people who collect them. Picture **Meenakshi-ji**, a government schoolteacher in a small town in Odisha, appointed as a census **enumerator** for a block of 150 houses.

In the first phase — **house-listing** — she walks every lane with a map, numbering each building with chalk: homes, shops, a temple, a half-built house. She notes what each house is made of, whether it has a tap, a toilet, electricity, a mobile phone, a bicycle.

Months later comes the main count — **population enumeration**. Over about three weeks she knocks on every door again. For each person she asks name, age, sex, relationship to the head of the household, marital status, religion, language, literacy, schooling, occupation, place of birth and whether they moved here from elsewhere — and why. A fisherman's family tells her their eldest son works in Chennai; she records him there, not here, because the census counts people **where they are found** on the reference date.

One evening she finds a family of seasonal brick-kiln workers living under tarpaulin near the highway. They are counted too — the census also counts **houseless** people on a special night.

All of Meenakshi-ji's forms join millions of others. Months later, the totals become the tables in your textbook: density, sex ratio, literacy. Every number you study is made of thousands of patient conversations like hers.

> *Did you know?* India's census is one of the largest administrative exercises in the world, involving roughly 25–30 lakh enumerators and supervisors.

check.q: Why is the census taken in two phases?
options: To count people twice for accuracy
First houses and amenities are listed, then every person is counted
Because the first phase is only for cities
check.why: The house-listing phase records buildings and amenities; the population enumeration phase records details of every person.

sections.md:
India's population in March 2011 stood at **1,210.6 million**, which is **17.5 per cent** of the world's population. These 1.21 billion people are **unevenly distributed** over our country's area of **3.28 million sq km**, which is **2.4 per cent** of the world's area. India has 2.4% of the land but 17.5% of the people!

The 2011 Census shows that:
- **Uttar Pradesh**, with **199 million** people, is the most populous state — about **16 per cent** of India's population.
- The Himalayan state **Sikkim** has only about **0.6 million** people, and **Lakshadweep** just **64,429**.
- Almost **half** of India's population lives in just **five states**: **Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh** (undivided).
- **Rajasthan**, the biggest state by area, has only **5.5 per cent** of the population.

**Population density** — the number of persons per unit area — measures this unevenness better. India is one of the most densely populated countries of the world. Its density in 2011 was **382 persons per sq km**, ranging from **1,102 in Bihar** to only **17 in Arunachal Pradesh**.

| Density level | Typical regions | Main reasons |
|---|---|---|
| Low (below about 250 per sq km) | Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Sikkim, Ladakh, western Rajasthan | Rugged mountains, dense forests, very dry or very cold climate |
| Moderate (about 250–500) | Assam and most Peninsular states | Hilly, dissected or rocky terrain; moderate to low rainfall; shallow, less fertile soils |
| High (above 500) | Northern Plains (UP, Bihar, West Bengal) and Kerala | Flat plains, fertile alluvial soils, abundant rainfall, more towns and jobs |

**Why so uneven?** Fertile plains, water, a pleasant climate and job opportunities in towns attract people. Mountains, deserts and dense forests discourage settlement. Kerala is an interesting case: it is not a great plain, but its coastal lowlands are fertile, rain is abundant, and its towns and villages run into each other in one long settled belt.

sections.md:
Population is dynamic. Its numbers, distribution and composition keep changing through three processes: **births, deaths and migration**.

**Growth** is the change in the number of inhabitants of a country during a specific period — say, the last 10 years. It can be expressed in two ways:
- **Absolute increase** — later population minus earlier population (e.g., 2011 minus 2001). It shows the magnitude of increase.
- **Annual growth rate** — in per cent per annum. A rate of 2% per annum means two persons are added each year for every 100 in the base population.

India's population rose steadily from **361 million in 1951 to 1,210 million in 2011**.

| Year | Population (million) | Annual growth rate in the decade ending (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 1951 | 361.1 | 1.25 |
| 1961 | 439.2 | 1.96 |
| 1971 | 548.2 | 2.20 |
| 1981 | 683.3 | 2.22 |
| 1991 | 846.4 | 2.14 |
| 2001 | 1,028.7 | 1.97 |
| 2011 | 1,210.6 | 1.64 |

**Reading the table:**
- From 1951 to 1981 the annual growth rate **kept rising**, so population nearly doubled, from 361 to 683 million.
- Since **1981**, the growth rate has **declined gradually** as birth rates fell.
- **Yet about 182 million people were added in 1991–2001**, and about 182 million again in 2001–2011. Why? When even a lower rate is applied to a very large base, it yields a large absolute increase.

**Population change vs population growth.** *Growth* is about numbers going up or down; *change* is broader — it includes shifts in distribution (where people live) and composition (age, sex, literacy) too.

> *Big update:* According to UN estimates, **India overtook China as the world's most populous country in 2023**.

check.q: Why did India add a huge number of people in the 1990s even though the growth rate was falling?
options: A lower rate applied to a very large base still gives a large absolute increase
check.why: Because India's base population was so large, even a smaller percentage growth produced a very large absolute increase.

sections.h: Processes of change: births, deaths, migration
sections.md:
**Natural increase** = birth rate − death rate.

- **Birth rate** — live births per thousand persons in a year. In India birth rates have always been higher than death rates.
- **Death rate** — deaths per thousand persons in a year. The main cause of India's fast growth has been the **rapid decline in death rates**, thanks to better medical care, vaccination, control of epidemics like smallpox and malaria, better famine relief and sanitation.

Till 1980, high birth rates and falling death rates created a wide gap, so growth was high. Since 1981, birth rates have also been falling, so growth has slowed.

**Migration** is the movement of people across regions and territories. It may be **internal** (within the country) or **international**. Internal migration **does not change the total size** of the population, but it changes its **distribution** within the nation, and the age and sex mix of both the places people leave and the places they reach.

In India most migration has been **rural to urban**, driven by the **push** of rural poverty and unemployment and the **pull** of urban jobs and better living conditions. The urban share of the population rose from **17.29 per cent in 1951 to 31.80 per cent in 2011**. The number of **million-plus cities** rose from **35 to 53** in just one decade (2001–2011).

> *Example:* A young man from a village in Bihar moves to Surat to work in a diamond-polishing unit. Push: little land, low farm wages. Pull: steady wages, relatives already there. His village's age–sex mix changes too — more women and elderly stay behind.
keyTerms: Birth rate — live births per 1,000 persons per year
Death rate — deaths per 1,000 persons per year
Natural increase — birth rate minus death rate
Migration — movement of people across regions
Million-plus city — city with over 10 lakh people

check.q: Internal migration within India changes which of these?
options: The total size of India's population
The distribution of population within the country
check.why: Internal migration moves people within the country, so it does not change India's total population but changes how it is distributed.

sections.md:
Why did India grow so fast after 1951 and then begin to slow? Population experts describe a pattern many countries pass through, often called the **demographic transition**. It is not in your textbook by that name, but it neatly explains the table you just read.

| Stage | Birth rate | Death rate | Growth | India's story |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | High | High | Slow | Before 1921: famines and epidemics kept deaths high |
| 2 | High | **Falling fast** | **Rapid** | 1921–1981: medicine, vaccines, famine relief cut deaths; births stayed high |
| 3 | **Falling** | Low | Slowing | 1981 onwards: education, especially of girls, urban living and family planning reduce births |
| 4 | Low | Low | Stable | Kerala and Tamil Nadu are close to this; India as a whole is approaching it |

The year **1921** is often called the *year of the great divide* in India's population history: before it, growth was slow and irregular; after it, population rose every single decade.

The gap between the two lines on the chart below is the **natural increase**. Notice how the gap widens and then narrows.

**What makes birth rates fall?** Several things together: girls staying longer in school and marrying later; fewer children dying young, so families no longer feel they need many births; access to health services and family-planning methods; urban life where children are costlier to raise; and better old-age security.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#f0fdf4'/><text x='300' y='24' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' font-weight='bold' fill='#14532d'>Birth rate vs death rate (schematic)</text><line x1='60' y1='260' x2='570' y2='260' stroke='#334155'/><line x1='60' y1='260' x2='60' y2='40' stroke='#334155'/><path d='M60,70 L200,72 L330,80 L450,150 L570,190' stroke='#16a34a' stroke-width='4' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='700' stroke-dashoffset='700'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' to='0' dur='3s' fill='freeze'/></path><path d='M60,80 L200,150 L330,210 L450,225 L570,228' stroke='#dc2626' stroke-width='4' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='700' stroke-dashoffset='700'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' to='0' dur='3s' begin='0.5s' fill='freeze'/></path><path d='M200,72 L330,80 L330,210 L200,150 Z' fill='#fde68a' opacity='0'><animate attributeName='opacity' to='0.7' begin='3.5s' dur='1s' fill='freeze'/></path><text x='265' y='130' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='11' fill='#7c2d12'>big gap = fast growth</text><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='11' fill='#334155' text-anchor='middle'><text x='130' y='280'>Stage 1</text><text x='265' y='280'>Stage 2</text><text x='390' y='280'>Stage 3</text><text x='510' y='280'>Stage 4</text></g><text x='520' y='182' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='11' fill='#16a34a'>births</text><text x='520' y='245' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='11' fill='#dc2626'>deaths</text></svg>
fig.caption: When deaths fall before births, the gap — natural increase — widens; as births fall too, it narrows.
fig.alt: Animated green birth-rate line and red death-rate line with the gap between them shaded.

check.q: In which stage was India between 1921 and about 1981?
check.why: Medical advances cut death rates while birth rates stayed high, so the natural increase was large.

sections.h: Characteristics: age, sex ratio, literacy, occupations, health
sections.md:
**Age composition** is the number of people in different age groups. Age shapes what people need, buy and do, and their capacity to work.

| Group | Age | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Children** | below 15 | Economically unproductive; need food, clothing, education, medical care |
| **Working age** | 15–59 | Economically productive and biologically reproductive |
| **Aged** | above 59 | May work voluntarily but usually retired from recruited jobs |

The share of children and the aged affects the **dependency ratio**, because these groups are not producers.

**Sex ratio** is the **number of females per 1,000 males**. It is an important social indicator of equality between men and women. India's sex ratio has always been **unfavourable to females**; in 2011 it was **940**. **Kerala** had **1,084** and **Puducherry** 1,038, while **Delhi** had only **866** and **Haryana** **877**. Low sex ratios reflect discrimination against girls, neglect of girls' health and sex-selective practices (which are illegal in India).

**Literacy.** Only informed, educated citizens can make wise decisions and drive research and development. Under Census 2011, a person aged **7 years and above** who can **read and write with understanding in any language** is literate. India's literacy rate was **74.04 per cent**: **82.14 per cent for males and 65.46 per cent for females** — a gap of about 17 points that shows how much remains to be done for girls' education.

**Occupational structure** — the distribution of people by type of work — is an index of development:
- **Primary**: agriculture, animal husbandry, forestry, fishing, mining and quarrying.
- **Secondary**: manufacturing, building and construction.
- **Tertiary**: transport, communications, commerce, administration and other services.

Developed nations have a high share of workers in secondary and tertiary activities; developing countries have more in primary activities. Your textbook notes that about **64 per cent** of India's population depended on agriculture, with a gradual shift towards industry and services as industrialisation and urbanisation grow (recent surveys put farming's share of the workforce at under half).

**Health.** Death rates fell from **25 per 1,000 in 1951 to 7.2 per 1,000 in 2011**, and **life expectancy at birth** rose from **36.7 years to 67.9 years**, thanks to better public health, prevention of infectious diseases and modern medicine. Yet concerns remain: calorie intake is below recommended levels for many, malnutrition is widespread, and safe drinking water and sanitation were long missing for much of rural India (programmes like Swachh Bharat and the Jal Jeevan Mission have since expanded access).

**Adolescents (10–19 years)** form about **one-fifth** of India's population — its most important resource for the future. Their nutritional needs are higher than those of children or adults, yet many diets are inadequate, and a large number of adolescent girls suffer from **anaemia**. Literacy and awareness are key to improving their well-being.

check.q: According to Census 2011, what was India's literacy rate?

check.q: What is the 'demographic dividend'?
options: Economic benefit when a large share of people are of working age and productively employed
check.why: When working-age people are many relative to dependants — and they are healthy, skilled and employed — the economy can grow faster.

sections.md:
**Map work.** On an outline map of India, show:
1. The state with the **highest** density (Bihar) and the **lowest** (Arunachal Pradesh).
2. The **most populous** state (Uttar Pradesh) and the **least populous** (Sikkim) — plus the UT Lakshadweep.
3. States with sex ratio **above 1,000** (Kerala; UT Puducherry).
4. Shade the five states that together hold about half the population.
Use darker shades for higher values — this kind of map is called a **choropleth**.

**Project 1 — My class census.** Collect (with permission, anonymously) each classmate's family size, ages of family members, whether anyone has moved from another state, and occupations of adults (primary/secondary/tertiary). Calculate your class's average family size, sex ratio and occupational mix. Compare with the 2011 national figures.

**Project 2 — Migration interview.** Talk to someone who moved to your town — a vegetable seller, a security guard, a neighbour. Ask (politely) where they came from, why, what was hard, and whether they send money home. Classify their reasons as push or pull factors.

**Project 3 — Debate.** 'A large population is India's greatest strength.' Prepare points for both sides using the burden/resource comparison above.

> *Exam tip:* For 'Why is the growth rate declining since 1981?', write: falling birth rates due to spread of education (especially of women), family-planning programmes, later marriages, urbanisation and lower infant mortality — and add that the absolute increase is still large because of the large base.

check.q: In a class survey, 21 girls and 24 boys are counted. What is the sex ratio?
check.why: Sex ratio = 21 ÷ 24 × 1,000 = 875 females per 1,000 males.

workedExamples.q: India's population was 1,028.7 million in 2001 and 1,210.6 million in 2011. Find the absolute increase.
A town has a birth rate of 22 per 1,000 and a death rate of 7 per 1,000. What is its rate of natural increase?
steps: Natural increase = birth rate − death rate.

workedExamples.q: A district has 4,20,000 males and 3,99,000 females. Calculate its sex ratio.
A state of area 94,000 sq km has a population of 10.4 crore. Find its density.
workedExamples.answer: About 1,106 persons per sq km — close to Bihar's figure.

workedExamples.q: A village has 300 children (below 15), 600 people aged 15–59 and 100 aged 60+. Find the dependency ratio.
workedExamples.answer: About 67 dependants for every 100 working-age people

summary: A census is an official count done every ten years; India's first complete census was in 1881.
In 2011 India had 1,210.6 million people — 17.5% of the world on 2.4% of its area.
Uttar Pradesh is most populous (199 million); Sikkim and Lakshadweep have very small populations; Rajasthan has only 5.5%.
Density in 2011 was 382 per sq km, from 1,102 in Bihar to 17 in Arunachal Pradesh.
Plains with fertile soils and rain (Northern Plains, Kerala) have high densities; hills, deserts and forests have low densities.
Growth is measured as absolute increase or annual growth rate; population change also includes distribution and composition.
Population rose from 361 million (1951) to 1,210 million (2011); the growth rate rose till 1981 and declined after.
Natural increase = birth rate − death rate; India's growth was driven by a rapid fall in death rates, later followed by falling birth rates.
Rural–urban migration (push and pull factors) raised the urban share from 17.29% (1951) to 31.80% (2011); million-plus cities rose from 35 to 53 (2001–2011).
Age groups: children (below 15), working age (15–59), aged (above 59).
Sex ratio in 2011 was 940; Kerala 1,084; Delhi 866; Haryana 877.
Literacy in 2011: 74.04% overall (males 82.14%, females 65.46%).
Occupations are primary, secondary and tertiary; India is shifting towards industry and services.
Death rate fell from 25 to 7.2 per 1,000 and life expectancy rose from 36.7 to 67.9 years (1951–2011).
Adolescents (10–19) are one-fifth of the population; NPP 2000 set goals on schooling, infant mortality, immunisation and delayed marriage.

rd-school-c9-social-c.ch1-what-is-democr.title: What is Democracy? Why Democracy?
rd-school-c9-social-c.ch1-what-is-democr.subtitle: Elections alone don't make a democracy. So what does — and why is it worth the trouble?

sections.h: A class election that went wrong
sections.md:
Imagine your school holds an election for class monitor. On the day of voting, the class teacher announces: *Only students who scored above 80 in maths may vote.* Another rule: *The current monitor can't be removed — he will stay for life.* A third: *Whoever wins must still get every decision approved by the principal's nephew.* Would you call this a democratic election? Probably not. Yet each rule only bends one thing a little.

That is exactly the puzzle of this chapter. Almost every government in the world today **claims** to be a democracy. Some hold elections where the result is already decided. Some let people vote but keep real power with the army. How do we tell real democracy from a fake one?

We will:
1. Start with a simple definition: **democracy is a form of government in which the rulers are elected by the people.**
2. Test it with real cases from around the world — and discover four features that a democracy must have.
3. Weigh the **arguments against and for** democracy.
4. Look at **broader meanings** of democracy, beyond government.

> *Origin of the word:* 'Democracy' comes from the Greek **demokratia** — *demos* (people) + *kratia* (rule). Rule by the people.

check.q: What does the Greek word 'demokratia' mean?
check.why: Demos means people and kratia means rule, so democracy literally means rule by the people.

sections.h: Why do we need a definition at all?
sections.md:
You might wonder why we need to define democracy. Isn't it obvious? But look at how differently people use the word:

- Some leaders say their country is a democracy because there is an election every five years — even if one party always wins.
- Some people say *democracy means majority rule*, so the minority must accept whatever the majority wants.
- Others say a country isn't truly democratic unless everyone has a decent income and education.

To avoid confusion, political scientists start with a **simple definition** and then sharpen it by testing it against real examples. The simple definition is:

> **Democracy is a form of government in which the rulers are elected by the people.**

This already tells us something important. It helps us separate democracies from obviously non-democratic governments:
- An **army ruler** (as in Myanmar after coups) is not elected by the people.
- A **monarch** such as the king of Saudi Arabia rules because he was born into the royal family, not because people chose him.
- A **one-party state** such as China's, where the Communist Party controls who can stand for office.

But the simple definition is not enough. Using it alone, we might accept a government as democratic merely because it holds some sort of election. So let us test it with real cases.

check.q: Which of these is NOT a democracy under even the simple definition?
options: A country where citizens elect the parliament
A country ruled by a hereditary king who is not elected
A country with regular elections between many parties
A country where the head of government is chosen by elected representatives
check.why: A hereditary monarch rules by birth, not because the people elected him, so it fails the simplest test of democracy.

sections.h: Feature 1: Major decisions by elected leaders
sections.md:
**The case of Pakistan, 1999.** In October 1999, **General Pervez Musharraf** led a military coup, overthrew the elected government and declared himself the 'Chief Executive'. Later he changed his designation to President, and in 2002 held a **referendum** in the country that granted him a five-year extension. Pakistani media, human rights organisations and democracy activists said that the referendum was based on malpractices and fraud.

In August 2002 he issued a 'Legal Framework Order' that **amended the Constitution of Pakistan**. According to this order, the President could **dismiss the national and provincial assemblies**. The work of the civilian cabinet was supervised by a **National Security Council**, which was dominated by military officers. After passing this law, elections were held to the national and provincial assemblies. So Pakistan had elections, elected representatives had some powers, but **the final power rested with military officers and General Musharraf himself**.

Would you call this a democracy? Clearly not. Though people elected the assemblies, the people who were elected were **not really the rulers**. They could not take the final decisions.

> **Feature 1:** In a democracy, the **final decision-making power must rest with those elected by the people**.

*Did you know?* Many countries have seen elected governments overruled by the army, by foreign powers, or by unelected bodies. That's why this feature is listed first.

check.q: Why was Pakistan under General Musharraf not a democracy even though elections were held?
options: Final power rested with the army and Musharraf, not elected representatives
check.why: Elected assemblies could be dismissed by the President and a military-dominated council supervised the cabinet, so elected leaders did not hold final power.

sections.h: Feature 2: Free and fair electoral competition
sections.md:
Many governments hold elections — but what kind of elections?

**China.** In China, elections are regularly held after every five years for electing the country's parliament, called the **Quanguo Renmin Daibiao Dahui** (National People's Congress). The National People's Congress has the power to appoint the President of the country. It has nearly **3,000 members** elected from all over China; some members are elected by the army. Before contesting elections, a candidate needs the **approval of the Chinese Communist Party**. Only those who are members of the Chinese Communist Party or **eight smaller parties allied to it** were allowed to contest elections. The government is always formed by the Communist Party.

**Mexico.** Mexico has held elections after every six years to elect its President since its independence in 1930. The country has never been under a military or dictator's rule. But until **2000** every election was won by a party called **PRI (Institutional Revolutionary Party)**. Opposition parties did contest elections, but never managed to win. The PRI was known to use many dirty tricks to win elections. All those who were employed in government offices had to attend its party meetings. Teachers of government schools used to force parents to vote for the PRI. Media largely ignored the activities of opposition political parties except to criticise them. Sometimes polling booths were shifted from one place to another in the last minute, which made it difficult for people to cast their votes. The PRI spent a large sum of money in the campaign for its candidates.

Should we treat these as democracies? People do vote — but they don't have a **real choice**. In China, voters can't choose a party other than the Communist Party or its allies. In Mexico, the playing field was tilted so heavily that the ruling party could not lose.

> **Feature 2:** A democracy must be based on a **free and fair election** where those currently in power have a **fair chance of losing**.

A free and fair election needs: a real choice between parties, freedom to campaign, independent election officials, no intimidation or bribery, and honest counting.

left.title: Not free and fair
points: Government staff forced to attend ruling party meetings (Mexico, before 2000)
Media ignores or attacks the opposition
Polling booths shifted at the last minute
Huge money power for the ruling party

right.title: Free and fair
points: Ruling party can — and sometimes does — lose

check.q: Why was Mexico before 2000 not considered a true democracy?
options: The PRI used unfair tricks so that it never lost
It was ruled by a king
check.why: Mexico held elections, but the ruling PRI's coercion, media control and booth-shifting meant it never had a fair chance of losing.

sections.h: Feature 3: One person, one vote, one value
sections.md:
We have seen that democracy is based on free and fair elections. But what if some people simply can't vote?

- Until **2015**, women in **Saudi Arabia** did not have the right to vote.
- **Estonia** made its citizenship rules in such a way that people belonging to the **Russian minority** find it difficult to get the right to vote.
- In **Fiji**, the electoral system is such that the vote of an indigenous Fijian has **more value** than that of an Indian-Fijian.

In each of these cases, elections exist, but the votes of some citizens either don't exist or count for less.

> **Feature 3:** In a democracy, **each adult citizen must have one vote and each vote must have one equal value**. This is called **universal adult franchise** — the principle of *one person, one vote, one value*.

This has a long history. In most democracies, at first only men who owned property could vote. Women, the poor, and minorities had to struggle for decades to win the vote. **New Zealand** was the first country to grant women the vote (1893). India, remarkably, gave **every adult citizen** — rich or poor, woman or man, literate or not — the right to vote from its **very first general election in 1951–52**, with the voting age at 21, later lowered to **18 in 1989**.
