emigrate — leave your country to settle in another
brood — think unhappily about something for a long time

check.q: Why did Anne feel lonely even though she had many friends?
options: She could only talk about ordinary things with them, never share deep feelings
check.why: Anne had thirty friends but no one to confide in, so she created 'Kitty' as a true friend in her diary.

sections.md:
**Scene 4 — the teachers' meeting.** Now the diary turns to school life, and anyone who has waited for exam results will recognise the scene. The whole class is terribly nervous. The teachers' meeting will decide who **moves up** to the next class and who is **kept back**.

Half the class is making bets. Anne and her friend G.Z. laugh at the two boys sitting behind them, C.N. and Jacques, who have bet their entire holiday savings on the result. From morning to night it's an endless back-and-forth — *you'll pass*, *no I won't*, *yes you will* — and neither Anne's pleading looks nor her angry outbursts can calm them down.

Anne's view is sensible and funny: there are so many lazy pupils in the class that perhaps a quarter of them deserve to be kept back, but teachers are the most **unpredictable creatures** on Earth — so maybe this time they will be unpredictable in the right direction.

She isn't too worried about her girlfriends and herself; they'll make it. The only subject she is unsure about is **maths**. All they can do is wait, and meanwhile they keep telling each other not to lose heart.

She gets along pretty well with all her teachers. There are nine of them — seven men and two women. And that brings us to the funniest part of the extract: **Mr Keesing**.

> Did you know? In the Dutch system of the time, 'forms' were school years; being 'kept back' meant repeating the year — just like being detained in an Indian school.

check.q: Which subject was Anne worried about?
check.why: Anne felt confident about her other subjects but was unsure about mathematics.

sections.h: Mr Keesing and the chatterbox essays
sections.md:
**Scene 5 — the punishment.** **Mr Keesing**, the old-fashioned maths teacher, was annoyed with Anne for ages because she **talked so much** in class. After several warnings, he gave her **extra homework**: an essay on the subject *'A Chatterbox'*.

**Essay 1 — 'A Chatterbox'.** What could anyone write about that? Anne wrote the title, chewed her pen, and thought. Then she had an idea. She filled **three pages** and was satisfied. Her argument: talking is a **student's trait**, and she would try to keep it under control — but she could never cure it completely, since her **mother talked as much as she did**, if not more. And what can you do about **inherited traits**? Mr Keesing had a good laugh at her arguments.

**Essay 2 — 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'.** When she went on talking in the next lesson, he set a second essay with this sterner title. She handed it in, and Mr Keesing had nothing to complain about for **two whole lessons**.

**Essay 3 — 'Quack, Quack, Quack, said Mistress Chatterbox'.** In the third lesson he'd had enough and gave her this title, meant as a joke at her expense. The class roared. Anne laughed too, but she had nearly run out of ideas on the subject. She decided to turn the joke back on him. Her friend **Sanne**, good at poetry, offered to help, and Anne wrote the whole essay **in verse**.

The poem told of a **mother duck and a father swan** with three baby ducklings, who were bitten to death by their father because they quacked too much. Mr Keesing **took the joke the right way**. He read the poem aloud to the class, adding his own comments, and to several other classes as well.

Since then Anne was allowed to talk, and she was **never given extra homework** again. On the contrary, Mr Keesing was always making jokes these days.

**Why was the poem so clever?** The 'father swan' who punishes chattering children stood for Mr Keesing himself. Anne showed him, gently and with humour, that punishing a child for a natural habit can be harsh. Because the message came wrapped in a joke, he could laugh instead of feeling insulted.

check.q: How did Anne finally win over Mr Keesing?
options: By writing a funny poem for the third essay
check.why: Her witty verse about ducks turned the joke back on him; he took it well and stopped punishing her.

sections.md:
**Anne Frank as revealed in the extract:**
- **Thoughtful and introspective** — she analyses her own loneliness honestly, and even admits it may be partly her fault.
- **Witty and clever** — the 'inherited trait' argument and the duck poem are brilliant comebacks.
- **Confident yet sensitive** — sure about her friends' promotion, nervous about maths, still missing her grandmother.
- **Mature beyond her years** — she sees the difference between many friends and one true friend.
- **Affectionate** — she calls her father the most adorable father and lights a candle for Grandma.

**Mr Keesing:**
- **Strict and old-fashioned** — he warns, then punishes, a talkative pupil.
- **Has a sense of humour** — he laughs at Essay 1 and invents a comic title for Essay 3.
- **Fair and open-minded** — when a pupil answers his punishment with wit, he reads her poem to several classes and changes his own behaviour.
- **A good teacher can learn from a student** — after the poem, he lets Anne talk and starts making jokes himself.

**Minor characters:** Margot (sister), Father and Mother, Grandmother (remembered with love), Sanne (friend who helps with the poem), G.Z. (friend), C.N. and Jacques (the anxious boys betting their savings).

check.q: Which quality of Mr Keesing is shown when he reads Anne's poem to other classes?
options: a good sense of humour and fairness
check.why: He could have been offended but instead enjoyed the joke against himself and stopped punishing her — he was fair and humorous.

sections.md:
1. **Loneliness and the need for a confidant.** Even popular people may feel alone. Many 'friends' are not the same as one person who understands you.
2. **Writing as healing.** A diary lets us sort out confused thoughts; putting feelings into words calms us.
3. **Student–teacher relationship.** Discipline mixed with humour works better than punishment alone. Respectful wit can solve a conflict.
4. **Adolescence.** Exam nerves, bets, friendships, teasing — the universal world of a 13-year-old.
5. **Childhood under a shadow.** The mention of emigration and the Jewish Lyceum reminds us of the persecution growing around her, even when she writes about ordinary things. This gives the cheerful extract a quiet sadness for readers who know her fate.

**Tone:** light, conversational, self-mocking and honest. **Style:** first person, informal, addressed to 'Kitty', as if chatting with a friend.

check.q: Which detail in the extract quietly hints at the persecution of Jews?
options: Anne moving to the Jewish Lyceum
check.why: Jewish children were forced out of ordinary schools, so Anne's move to the Jewish Lyceum reflects the anti-Jewish laws.

sections.h: Thinking about language: idioms, phrasal verbs, compounds
sections.md:
**1. Compound words.** A compound is two words joined to make one meaning: *heart-broken*, *homesick*, *blackboard*, *short-sighted*, *bad-tempered*, *notebook*, *birthday*. They can be nouns, adjectives or verbs. Exercise type: *find compounds in a list and say what part of speech they are*, e.g. **homesick** (adjective, missing home), **blackmail** (verb/noun), **heart-broken** (adjective, very sad).

**2. Idioms** from or connected with the text:
- *nothing to write home about* — not special
- *to get something off one's chest* — to talk about a worry so you feel better
- *to quake in one's boots* — to be very frightened
- *to keep a straight face* — not to laugh
- *to make a joke at someone's expense* — to tease
- *to lose heart* — to become discouraged

**3. Phrasal verbs** (verb + particle, with a new meaning):
- *plunge in* — begin suddenly
- *kept back* — not promoted
- *move up* — be promoted
- *ramble on* — talk for a long time
- *get along with* — have a good relationship with
- *calm down* — become quiet
- *stay in* — remain at home
- *make up for* — compensate
- *hand in* — submit

**4. Speaking and writing tasks.** The chapter suggests (a) a discussion on keeping a diary and on whether teachers should punish talking, and (b) a short piece of writing — for example a diary entry about your own exam results or your first day at a new school. Use first person, date it, write as if to a friend.
keyTerms: idiom — a phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its words
phrasal verb — verb + adverb/preposition with a special meaning
compound — two words joined into one

check.q: 'The students were quaking in their boots before the results.' This means they were…
check.why: To quake in one's boots is an idiom meaning to be very afraid.

sections.md:
**Q. Why does Anne want to keep a diary?** (30–40 words) Anne has no true friend to confide in. Paper is patient and does not judge, so she decides to make her diary her friend, name it Kitty, and pour out her thoughts and feelings in it.

**Q. How did Anne justify being a chatterbox?** She argued that talking is a student's trait and that she had inherited it from her mother, who talked as much as she did. One cannot do much about inherited traits — so she could only try to control it.

**Q. Was Mr Keesing a good teacher? (long answer, 120 words)** Mr Keesing was strict: he warned Anne repeatedly and then set punishment essays. Yet he was not unkind. He laughed at her clever first essay, and even his third title was a joke rather than an insult. When Anne replied with a poem about a swan who killed his chattering ducklings, he understood that the joke was on him — and he took it well, reading it to several classes. After that he let her talk and began joking himself. A teacher who can accept criticism from a pupil and change his behaviour shows humility, humour and fairness. So he was, in the end, a good teacher.

**Q. What does the extract tell us about Anne's family?** Her father was loving; parents married when he was 36 and she 25; Margot was born in 1926; they moved from Frankfurt to Holland in 1933 because they were Jewish; Grandma lived with them and died in January 1942.

**Value point:** honest self-expression, using humour instead of rudeness, and the power of writing.

parts.md: Ritika, a Class 10 student in Pune, had sixty followers on a photo app and a crowded group chat, but on the night before her pre-boards she felt nobody really knew her. Remembering the Anne Frank chapter, she pulled out an old notebook and wrote 'Dear Kitty' — then crossed it out and wrote 'Dear Tara', after her late grandmother. The words came easily: fear of chemistry, a fight with her best friend, how she still kept Tara-dadi's shawl in her cupboard.

Weeks later her strict maths teacher assigned her an essay as punishment for talking: 'Why I Talk Too Much'. Ritika smiled and wrote a rhyming answer about a mynah who was told to stop singing — and whose silence made the whole garden sad. Her teacher read it aloud, laughed, and said, 'Anne Frank would approve.' Ritika understood then what the chapter teaches: paper is patient, and a clever, kind answer can change even a teacher's mind.

summary: Extract from Anne Frank's diary, written in June 1942 in Amsterdam, before the family went into hiding.
Pre-reading: diary (private, daily), journal, log (factual), memoir (looking back).
Anne got the diary on her 13th birthday (12 June 1942).
'Paper has more patience than people' — a diary listens without judging.
Anne has family and about thirty friends but no true friend to confide in.
She names her diary 'Kitty' and treats it as her real friend.
Brief history: parents married when father was 36, mother 25; Margot born 1926; Anne born 1929; moved to Holland in 1933.
Grandmother died in January 1942; Anne still loves and misses her.
She moved from the Montessori school to the Jewish Lyceum — a sign of anti-Jewish laws.
Class anxious about promotion; Anne worried only about maths.
Mr Keesing, maths teacher, punished her talking with essays.
Essay 1: chattering is inherited from her mother; Essay 2: 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'.
Essay 3: a poem about ducks and a swan, written with Sanne's help; Keesing took the joke well.
Anne was then allowed to talk; shows her wit and a teacher's good humour.
Language: compound words, idioms, phrasal verbs (plunge in, kept back, hand in…).

rd-school-c10-english-a.ff-glimpses-indi.subtitle: Bread from Goa, coffee hills of Coorg, tea gardens of Assam — three windows on one country

sections.h: A hook: three journeys in one chapter
sections.md:
If you could take a train from the Konkan coast down to the Western Ghats and then fly to the Brahmaputra valley, what would you taste, smell and hear? *Glimpses of India* takes you on exactly that trip in three short pieces:

1. **A Baker from Goa** by **Lucio Rodrigues** — a warm, nostalgic memory of the village baker (*pader*) in Portuguese-influenced Goa.
2. **Coorg** by **Lokesh Abrol** — a travel essay on the misty coffee land of Kodagu in Karnataka, its brave people and wildlife.
3. **Tea from Assam** by **Arup Kumar Datta** — two boys on a train to Assam, the legends of tea, and a visit to a tea estate.

Each piece is a different kind of writing: a memoir, a descriptive travelogue, and a short story with facts. Together they show India's **diversity** — food, landscape, history and work.

These are recent, copyrighted pieces, so this companion retells and explains them in our own words; read the exact text in the free official NCERT PDF (link at the end).

sections.h: Part I — A Baker from Goa: the jingle of the bamboo
sections.md:
The writer begins with elders in Goa who are nostalgic about the good old **Portuguese days**, the Portuguese and their famous **loaves of bread**. Those eaters of loaves may have vanished, but the **makers** are still there. The mixers, the moulders and those who bake the loaves still exist in Goa, and so does the time-honoured furnace. Even now, in some places, the son carries on the father's trade — the **thud and jingle** of the traditional bamboo staff still announces the baker's arrival.

The author remembers childhood mornings. The baker (*pader*) was their friend, companion and guide. He came **at least twice a day**: once when he set out on his selling round in the morning, and again when he returned after emptying his huge basket. The jingling thud of his bamboo woke the children from sleep, and they ran to meet him.

Why were they so excited? Not for the loaves — those were for the maid-servant of the house — but for the **bread-bangles**, which they chose carefully. Sometimes it was sweet bread of special make.

The baker entered with the musical *jhang, jhang* of his bamboo. One hand supported the basket on his head, the other banged the bamboo on the ground. He greeted the lady of the house and placed his basket on the vertical bamboo. The children were pushed aside with a mild scolding, and the loaves were delivered to the servant. But the children would not give up; they climbed a bench or the parapet and peeped into the basket. The author can still recall the typical **fragrance** of those loaves. Often they did not even brush their teeth properly first — and why bother? he jokes, comparing the children to a tiger that never brushes its teeth.

check.q: What did the children look forward to when the baker came?
check.why: The loaves were for the household servant; the children eagerly chose the sweet bread-bangles for themselves.

sections.h: Part I — bread at every occasion
sections.md:
In Goa, bread was part of **every important occasion**:

- **Marriage gifts** are meaningless without the sweet bread called the **bol**.
- **Cakes and bolinhas** are a must for **Christmas** and other festivals.
- The lady of the house must prepare **sandwiches** on the occasion of her daughter's engagement.

So the presence of the baker's furnace in the village was **absolutely essential**.

**The baker's dress** was peculiar. It was known as the **kabai** — a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees. In the author's childhood, bakers wore a shirt and trousers shorter than full-length and longer than half pants. Even today, anyone wearing a half-pant that reaches just below the knees invites the comment that he is dressed like a *pader*.

**Monthly accounts.** The baker usually collected his bills at the end of the month. **Monthly accounts were recorded on some wall in pencil**.

**Prosperity.** Baking was indeed a profitable profession in the old days. The baker and his family never starved. He, his family and his servants always looked happy and prosperous. Their **plump physique** was an open testimony to this. Even today, any person with a jackfruit-like physical appearance is easily compared to a baker.

The writing is affectionate and gently humorous. It is a **memoir** that celebrates a community's way of life.
keyTerms: pader — Goan baker
bol — sweet bread essential for weddings
bolinhas — small cakes for festivals
kabai — the baker's knee-length frock
furnace — oven for baking

check.q: Where did the baker record monthly accounts?
check.why: The text recalls that the baker's monthly bills were noted in pencil on some wall of the house.

sections.h: Part I — tone, themes and language work
sections.md:
**Tone:** nostalgic, warm and humorous. The writer is not just describing bread; he is mourning — gently — a disappearing way of village life while celebrating that it still survives.

**Themes:**
- **Tradition and continuity** — the son carries on the father's trade; the furnace is 'time-honoured'.
- **Cultural blending** — Portuguese bread became truly Goan, woven into Indian weddings and Christian festivals alike.
- **Childhood joy** — the baker was a friend, and his bamboo's jingle was the sound of morning.
- **Community** — trust-based credit on the wall, the baker known to every family.

**Thinking about language (exercise types):**
1. *Used to / would* for past habits: 'The baker **used to** come twice a day.' 'We **would** run to meet him.' Both show repeated actions in the past; *would* cannot be used for past states ('He used to be plump', not 'He would be plump').
2. *Simple past vs present perfect*: the elders **have lost** the Portuguese days; the makers **are** still there.
3. Words and phrases: *nostalgic*, *time-honoured*, *testimony*, *physique*, *jackfruit-like* (a playful simile for a round, plump body).

**Is it a happy picture?** Yes. Every detail — the musical *jhang jhang*, the fragrance, the bangles, the plump prosperous family — is cheerful. Even the jokes (the tiger, the kabai) are affectionate.

check.q: Which sentence uses 'would' correctly for a past habit?
options: Every morning we would run to the baker.
Goa would be a Portuguese colony.
I would have a bicycle as a child.
check.why: 'Would' can describe repeated past actions like running to meet the baker, but not past states such as being plump or owning something.

sections.h: Part II — Coorg: a piece of heaven
sections.md:
Midway between **Mysore** and the coastal town of **Mangalore** sits a land so lovely that the writer imagines it drifted down from heaven. This land of rolling hills is home to a proud race of **martial men, beautiful women and wild creatures**.

**Coorg (Kodagu)** is the **smallest district of Karnataka**. It is home to evergreen rainforests, spices and **coffee plantations**. Evergreen rainforests cover thirty per cent of the district. During the **monsoon**, it pours enough to keep many visitors away. The season of joy starts from **September** and continues till **March**. The weather is perfect, with some showers thrown in for good measure. The air smells of fresh coffee. Coffee estates and colonial bungalows stand tucked under tree canopies in prime corners.

**The people.** The fiercely independent people of Coorg are possibly of **Greek or Arabic descent**. As one story goes, a part of **Alexander's army** moved south along the coast and settled here when return became impractical. These people married amongst the locals, and their culture is apparent in their martial traditions, marriage and religious rites, which are distinct from the Hindu mainstream. The theory of Arab origin draws support from the long, black coat with an embroidered waist-belt worn by the Kodavus, known as **kuppia**, which resembles the *kuffia* worn by Arabs and Kurds. (The text presents both as stories/theories, not proven facts.)

**Hospitality and valour.** Coorgi homes have a tradition of hospitality, and they are more than willing to recount numerous tales of valour related to their sons and fathers. The **Coorg Regiment** is one of the most decorated in the Indian Army, and the first Chief of the Indian Army, **General Cariappa**, was a Coorgi. Even now, Kodavus are the only people in India permitted to carry firearms without a licence.

sections.h: Part II — rivers, adventure and wildlife
sections.md:
**The River Kaveri** obtains its water from the hills and forests of Coorg. **Mahaseer** — a large freshwater fish — abound in these waters. **Kingfishers** dive for their catch, while squirrels and langurs drop partially eaten fruit for the fun of the splash in the clear water. Wild **elephants** enjoy being bathed and scrubbed in the river by their mahouts.

**Adventure.** Even the most relaxed visitors are tempted into high-energy adventure with **river rafting, canoeing, rappelling, rock climbing and mountain biking**. Numerous walking trails are a favourite with trekkers.

**Birds and animals.** Birds, bees and butterflies are there to give you company. **Macaques, Malabar squirrels, langurs and slender loris** keep a watchful eye from the tree canopy. Elephants are also present.

**Brahmagiri hills.** Climb the Brahmagiri hills to get a panoramic view of the entire misty landscape of Coorg. A walk across the rope bridge leads to the sixty-four-acre island of **Nisargadhama**.

**Buddhism.** Running into **Buddhist monks** from India's largest Tibetan settlement, at **Bylakuppe**, near Kushalnagar, is a bonus. The monks, in red, ochre and yellow robes, are among the many surprises waiting for visitors searching for the heart and soul of India in Coorg.

**Getting there.** Coorg is about 250–260 km by road from Bangalore. The nearest airports are Mangalore and Bangalore; the nearest railheads are Mysore, Mangalore and Hassan.

**Writing style:** notice the travel-brochure tone — superlatives (*smallest, most decorated, largest*) and vivid sensory details (the air that smells of coffee, mist drifting over hills).

sections.h: Part II — language work: collocations and idioms
sections.md:
The Coorg exercises focus on **collocations** — words that naturally go together — and on lively phrases.

**Collocations:** we say *heavy rain* (not 'strong rain'), *strong coffee* (not 'heavy coffee'), *a piece of heaven*, *tales of valour*, *a proud race*, *high-energy adventure*, *a watchful eye*, *prime corners*. A good exercise: match *heavy* and *strong* with nouns — heavy traffic, heavy luggage; strong wind, strong tea, strong opinion.

**Phrases from the text, explained:**
- *drifted from the kingdom of God* — so beautiful it seems heavenly (hyperbole)
- *thrown in for good measure* — added as an extra
- *the most laid-back* — the most relaxed, unhurried
- *converts to* — people who have changed to a new way of life
- *keep a watchful eye* — observe carefully
- *a bonus* — an extra pleasure

**Why it is a travelogue:** it gives location, best season, people, history, activities, sights and how to get there — everything a traveller wants — in attractive language.
keyTerms: collocation — words that habitually go together
hyperbole — deliberate exaggeration for effect
travelogue — writing about a journey or a place

check.q: Which is the correct collocation?
check.why: In English we naturally say heavy rain and heavy traffic, but strong coffee and strong wind.

sections.h: Part III — Tea from Assam: on the train
sections.md:
**Rajvir** and his friend **Pranjol** are travelling by train to Assam. Pranjol is from Assam; his father is a manager of a tea garden in **Upper Assam**, and Rajvir is going there for the summer vacation.

A vendor comes calling *chai-garam… garam-chai*, and the boys order two cups. Rajvir remarks that over **80 crore cups of tea** are drunk every day throughout the world — an amazing figure! Pranjol is busy reading a detective book and pays little attention.

The train passes through lush green landscape. Then Rajvir sees, as far as the eye can see, **tea bushes** — a sea of green, with tall shade-trees standing among the neat rows and tiny, doll-like figures moving busily between them. In the distance stands an ugly building with smoke pouring out of tall chimneys. *A tea garden!* Rajvir cries excitedly. Pranjol, who was born and brought up on a plantation, isn't impressed.

Rajvir tells his friend that Assam has the **largest concentration of plantations in the world**. Pranjol replies drily that Rajvir will see enough gardens to last him a lifetime.

Rajvir had read up about tea before coming. He knows a lot — and shares it in the form of **two legends**.

check.q: Why was Pranjol not as excited as Rajvir on seeing the tea garden?
options: He was born and brought up on a tea plantation
check.why: Tea gardens were an everyday sight for Pranjol, who grew up on one, so he found nothing special about them.

sections.h: Part III — legends of tea and the tea estate
sections.md:
Rajvir explains that no one really knows who discovered tea, but there are many legends.

**The Chinese legend.** A Chinese emperor always boiled water before drinking it. One day a few leaves of the twigs burning under the pot fell into the water, giving it a delicious flavour. It is said they were tea leaves.

**The Indian legend.** **Bodhidharma**, an ancient Buddhist ascetic, cut off his eyelids because he felt sleepy during meditations. Ten tea plants grew out of the eyelids. The leaves of these plants, when put in hot water and drunk, banished sleep.

**History.** Tea was first drunk in **China** as far back as **2700 BC**. In fact, words such as *tea, chai* and *chini* are from Chinese. Tea came to **Europe** only in the **sixteenth century** and was drunk more as a **medicine** than as a beverage.

**At the estate.** The train reaches **Mariani junction**. The boys get off, and Pranjol's parents meet them. They drive towards **Dhekiabari**, the tea estate Pranjol's father manages. On both sides of the gravel road are acres of tea bushes, all neatly pruned to the same height. Groups of **tea-pluckers**, with bamboo baskets on their backs and wearing plastic aprons, are plucking the newly sprouted leaves.

Pranjol's father explains that it is the **second-flush** or sprouting period, which lasts from **May to July** and yields the **best tea**. Rajvir surprises him by saying he knows this already. The chapter ends with Rajvir enthusiastically planning to see everything.

sections.h: Part III — from leaf to cup, and language work
sections.md:
The story stops at the garden, but exam questions often ask what Rajvir would see next. In simple terms, plucked leaves go to the **factory** (the 'ugly building with chimneys'): they are **withered** (dried slightly), **rolled**, **oxidised/fermented** (they turn dark), **dried** in hot air, then **sorted and packed**. That is why a tea estate has both gardens and a factory.

**Characters:** *Rajvir* — curious, well-read, enthusiastic, prepares before travelling. *Pranjol* — relaxed, used to tea gardens, a little bored by Rajvir's facts but friendly. *Pranjol's father* — welcoming, informative.

**Language work (exercise types):**
1. **Passive voice** for facts and processes: 'Tea **was first drunk** in China.' 'The leaves **are plucked** by hand.' 'The bushes **are pruned** to the same height.' We use the passive when the action matters more than who does it.
2. **Words from Chinese:** tea, chai, chini — a nice note on how words travel with things.
3. **Phrases:** *as far as the eye could see*, *enough to last a lifetime*, *read up on* (study a topic in advance).

**Themes across all three parts:** India's diversity; how food and drink carry history (Portuguese bread, coffee estates, Chinese tea); pride in one's region; and the pleasure of travel and curiosity.

sections.md:
**Q. How do we know that bread is an important part of Goan life?** Bread marks every occasion: the bol is a must as a marriage gift, cakes and bolinhas are essential at Christmas, and sandwiches are prepared for a daughter's engagement. A village without a baker's furnace is unthinkable.

**Q. Describe the baker's arrival in the author's childhood.** The thud and jingle of his bamboo woke the children. Balancing the basket on his head with one hand and banging the bamboo with the other, he greeted the lady of the house, gave the loaves to the servant and let the children pick bread-bangles while they peeped eagerly into the basket.

**Q. What are the main attractions of Coorg? (120 words)** Coorg, the smallest district of Karnataka, lies between Mysore and Mangalore. Its hills are covered with rainforest and coffee estates, and the air smells of coffee. September to March is the best season. Its people, the Kodavus, are proud and brave, possibly of Greek or Arab descent; the Coorg Regiment and General Cariappa make them famous. The Kaveri offers mahaseer fish, kingfishers and elephants being bathed. Visitors enjoy rafting, canoeing, rappelling, rock climbing, mountain biking and trekking, a view from the Brahmagiri hills, the island of Nisargadhama and the Tibetan monks of Bylakuppe.

**Q. Why is the second flush important?** The second flush (May–July) is the second sprouting of leaves and yields the best-quality tea, so it is the most valuable plucking season.

summary: Three pieces: A Baker from Goa (Lucio Rodrigues), Coorg (Lokesh Abrol), Tea from Assam (Arup Kumar Datta).
Goan bakers (paders) continue a Portuguese-era tradition; the bamboo's jingle announces them.
Children loved the bread-bangles; loaves went to the servant.
Bread is essential at Goan occasions: bol for weddings, cakes and bolinhas for Christmas, sandwiches for engagements.
Bakers wore the kabai; accounts were written on walls in pencil; bakers looked plump and prosperous.
Language in Part I: used to / would for past habits.
Coorg (Kodagu), smallest district of Karnataka, between Mysore and Mangalore; coffee, rainforests, best season Sept–March.
Kodavus may be of Greek or Arab descent (theories); kuppia resembles the Arab kuffia.
Coorg Regiment highly decorated; General Cariappa was a Coorgi; Kodavus may carry firearms without licence.
Kaveri, mahaseer, kingfishers, elephants; adventure sports; Brahmagiri, Nisargadhama, Bylakuppe monks.
Language in Part II: collocations (heavy rain, strong coffee) and lively phrases.
Rajvir and Pranjol travel to Assam; Assam has the world's largest concentration of tea plantations.
Legends: Chinese emperor's leaves; Bodhidharma's eyelids. Tea drunk in China from 2700 BC; reached Europe in the 16th century as medicine.
Dhekiabari estate; second flush (May–July) yields the best tea.
Language in Part III: passive voice for facts and processes.

rd-school-c10-english-a.ff-letter-to-god.title: A Letter to God — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-a.ff-letter-to-god.subtitle: A farmer, a hailstorm, a letter addressed to heaven — and a post office that answered

sections.h: A hook: who reads a letter addressed to God?
sections.md:
Imagine you work at the village post office. One morning a letter arrives. The envelope is written in a careful, slow hand, and the address says simply: **To God**. There is no street, no PIN code, no city. What would you do? Laugh? Throw it away? Open it?

This is the starting puzzle of *A Letter to God*, a short story by the Mexican writer **G. L. Fuentes** (Gregorio López y Fuentes, 1897–1966). Fuentes wrote about rural Mexico — farmers, fields, rain and the hard life of people who depend completely on the weather. The story is short, but it holds three big ideas that examiners love:

- **Faith** — a deep, simple, unshakeable trust in God.
- **Kindness** — strangers who quietly help someone they have never met.
- **Irony** — the twist that the man who is helped suspects the very people who helped him.

Because Fuentes died in 1966 and the English translation is still in copyright, this companion retells the story scene by scene in our own words — read the exact text in the free NCERT PDF linked at the end. We will look at each character, unpack the language, and finish with exam-ready answers.

> Did you know? Fuentes won Mexico's first National Prize for Literature in 1935 for his novel *El Indio*, about the lives of indigenous people.

sections.h: Before you read: faith and the farmer
sections.md:
The textbook opens with a question to think about: *Have you ever trusted completely that something would work out, even when there was no proof?* That is the kind of trust — **faith** — this story is about.

It also helps to know the setting. Rural Mexico, like rural India, has millions of small farmers who grow **maize (corn)** and **beans** on rain-fed land. They have no canals or borewells; the sky is their irrigation. The money in the story is the **peso**, Mexico's currency (like our rupee).

Keep three questions in mind as you read, because the exercises ask them in different forms:
1. What does Lencho hope for, and what destroys his hope?
2. Whom does Lencho trust, and how does he show it?
3. Who actually helps him, and how does he react?

check.q: What is the currency used in the story?
check.why: The story is set in Mexico, whose currency is the peso; Lencho asks God for a hundred pesos.

sections.h: The setting: a house on a hill and a field of corn
sections.md:
**Scene 1.** The story opens in a lonely house standing on the crest of a low hill — the **only** house in the whole valley. From there the farmer, **Lencho**, can see the river and his field of ripe **corn**, dotted with the flowers of **beans** that always promise a good harvest.

For a farmer in such a place, everything depends on one thing: **rain**. In India we understand this instantly. Think of a farmer in Vidarbha or Bundelkhand watching the sky in June, waiting for the monsoon. One good shower can mean school fees, new clothes for Diwali, and seed for next year. One bad storm can wipe all of that away.

Lencho knows his land well. He looks towards the north-east and sees huge mountains of clouds approaching. He is delighted. He tells his wife that the raindrops are not water but **new coins** — the big drops are ten-cent pieces and the little ones are fives. This tiny detail tells us a lot: Lencho is an experienced farmer, he thinks in terms of money and survival, and he is hopeful by nature.

Notice the family: his wife is preparing supper, the older boys are working in the field, and the little ones are playing. It is a picture of an ordinary, happy, hard-working family. Fuentes builds this calm on purpose — so that the storm that follows feels even more cruel.

check.q: Why does Lencho compare the raindrops to new coins?
options: He collects coins as a hobby
Rain will help his crop and so bring him money
The drops shine like silver in sunlight
check.why: For a farmer, good rain means a good harvest and therefore income, so every drop feels like money falling from the sky.

sections.h: The storm: from joy to ruin
sections.md:
**Scene 2.** At first the rain falls gently and Lencho steps outside just to enjoy it. Then a strong wind begins to blow, and with the rain come very large **hailstones**. The children run out to collect the frozen pearls, thinking it fun. But for the next hour the hail falls on the house, the garden, the hillside, the cornfield, the whole valley. The field turns white, as though salt had been spread over it.

When the storm passes, not a leaf remains on the trees. The corn is destroyed. The flowers have been knocked off the bean plants. Lencho's soul is filled with sadness. He tells his family that a plague of **locusts** would have left more than this — the hail has left nothing. They will have no corn that year.

This is the emotional low point of the story. The family faces hunger, and the night that follows is full of sorrow.

But even here, in the middle of despair, there is one small light. The family members comfort one another with the belief that no one dies of hunger, and they hold on to the single hope they have: **help from God**. Lencho's wife and children are just as faithful as he is.

**Language note:** comparing the white field to one covered with salt is a **simile** — a comparison using *as* or *like*. Salt also suggests barrenness: in old stories, salting a field meant nothing would ever grow there again.

> Did you know? Hail forms when strong upward winds inside a thundercloud carry raindrops high into freezing air again and again, adding layers of ice each time, until the stone is too heavy and falls.

**Scene 3.** All night Lencho thinks of only one thing — his hope in God, whose eyes, he has been taught, see everything, even what lies deep in a person's conscience. Lencho is described as **an ox of a man**, working like an animal in the fields, yet he knows how to write.

The following Sunday, at daybreak, he sits down to write a letter that he himself will carry into town and post. In our own words, the letter says something like: *God, if you don't help me, my family and I will go hungry this year. I need a hundred pesos to sow my field again and to live until the new crop comes, because the hailstorm…*

He writes **To God** on the envelope, puts the letter inside, and goes to town. At the post office he places a stamp on it and drops it into the mailbox.

Pause on this moment. A modern reader may find it funny or innocent. But think again: Lencho does not beg from neighbours, does not steal, does not give up. He calmly writes a request to the one power he trusts completely. His faith is **practical** — he does exactly what one would do to contact anyone far away: write, stamp, post.

The amount is important too. He asks for **100 pesos** — a specific amount for a specific purpose: to sow again and survive until the next harvest. He is not greedy.

check.q: What does the phrase 'an ox of a man' suggest about Lencho?
options: He is strong, hard-working and simple
check.why: An ox works tirelessly in the field; calling Lencho 'an ox of a man' stresses his physical toil and simple nature.

sections.h: The post office: kindness without a name
sections.md:
**Scene 4.** One of the employees, a **postman** who also helps at the post office, finds the letter and goes laughing to his boss, the **postmaster**. In all his years he has never seen such an address.

The postmaster — described as a fat, friendly fellow — also laughs at first. But then he becomes serious. Tapping the letter, he says, in effect, that he wishes he had the faith of the man who wrote it — imagine starting a correspondence with God!

This is the turning point of the story. The postmaster decides that this faith must not be shaken. He chooses to **answer** the letter. But when he opens it, he realises that answering needs more than goodwill — it needs money, which he does not have.

So he asks his employees for help. He gives **part of his own salary**. Several friends also give something *for an act of charity*. Even with all this, he cannot collect the full hundred pesos. He manages to gather **a little more than half**. He puts the money in an envelope addressed to Lencho and, with it, a letter signed with just one word: **God**.

Notice how quiet this generosity is. Nobody seeks credit. The postmaster even signs as God so that Lencho's faith stays whole. This is kindness at its purest: helping a stranger and remaining unknown.

check.q: Why did the postmaster sign the letter as 'God'?
options: He wanted to play a joke
He did not want to shake Lencho's faith in God
He was ordered to by the government
check.why: The postmaster admired Lencho's faith and wanted him to believe that God had answered, so he hid his own role.

sections.md:
**Scene 5.** The next Sunday Lencho comes a little earlier than usual to ask whether there is a letter for him. The postman himself hands it over, while the postmaster watches from his office door with the quiet happiness of a man who has done a good deed.

Lencho shows **not the slightest surprise** on seeing the money — that is how complete his faith is. Of course God answered. But when he counts the money, he becomes **angry**. God could not have made a mistake, nor could He have refused what Lencho asked for. Lencho has received only **70 pesos** — so, in his mind, **30 pesos** have gone missing somewhere on the way.

He goes to the window, asks for paper and ink, and at the public writing table he writes a second letter, frowning with concentration. He sticks the stamp on with a blow of his fist and drops it in the mailbox.

As soon as it falls in, the postmaster opens it. In our words, it says: *God, of the money I asked for, only seventy pesos reached me. Send me the rest, since I need it very much. But don't send it through the mail, because the post-office employees are dishonest.* It is signed **Lencho**. (His actual phrase for them — 'a bunch of crooks' — is the one line everyone remembers.)

This is the great **irony** of the story. The very people who sacrificed their own salaries to help him are the ones he calls thieves. The reader knows the truth; Lencho does not. That gap between what a character believes and what the reader knows is called **dramatic irony**.

The story ends right there — we never see the postmaster's face. Fuentes leaves the reader to feel the sting and the humour together.
keyTerms: irony — when the result is the opposite of what is expected
dramatic irony — the reader knows something a character does not
amiable — friendly and pleasant

check.q: How much money did Lencho receive?
check.why: Lencho's second letter says only seventy pesos reached him, which was a little more than half of what he asked.

sections.md:
**Lencho** — a hard-working farmer, simple, honest and deeply religious. He can read and write. His faith is so complete that he is not surprised when the money arrives; it is also so blind that he cannot imagine humans helped him, and he wrongly suspects them. He is also a little ungrateful — but from his point of view, he is only being honest with God.

**Lencho's wife and children** — share his faith and his hardship. They are a picture of the farming family who lives from season to season.

**The postmaster** — kind, generous, thoughtful. He laughs at first but quickly recognises the beauty of Lencho's faith. He gives from his own salary, organises a collection, and protects Lencho's belief by signing as God. He represents **humanity's goodness**.

**The post office employees and friends** — they contribute for an act of charity without knowing Lencho. They prove that God's help often comes through ordinary people.

A useful way to remember the theme is the phrase: **God helps through humans.** Lencho asked God; God's answer came through a postmaster's pocket.

**1. Faith** — Lencho's faith is the engine of the story. It gives him hope after disaster and makes him write the letter. The postmaster says he wishes he had such faith.

**2. Humanity and charity** — strangers help without reward. The story suggests that goodness is real, even if it goes unrecognised.

**3. Irony** — the helpers are called crooks. This makes the story memorable and slightly comic.

**4. Nature's power** — one hour of hail undoes a season's work. Farmers all over the world, including India, live with this risk; that is why schemes like crop insurance exist.

**5. Innocence vs experience** — Lencho's faith is childlike; the postmaster's is the wistful admiration of an educated man who has lost such certainty.

**The title** *A Letter to God* is apt because the whole plot turns on that letter: it shows Lencho's faith, triggers the postmaster's kindness, and the second letter creates the ironic ending.

**Exam tip:** In long answers, always connect a theme to an event. E.g. 'Lencho's faith is shown when he shows not the slightest surprise on receiving money.'

> Did you know? Postal services in many countries — including India Post — really do receive letters addressed to God, to Santa Claus or to temples. Some are answered by volunteers.

check.q: What is the main irony in the story?
options: The people who helped Lencho were called crooks by him
check.why: The postmaster and staff gave their own money, yet Lencho accused them of stealing part of it — the opposite of the truth.

sections.h: Language corner: words, phrases and grammar
sections.md:
The NCERT exercises on this chapter focus on a few language skills. Here is what to master.

**Words with more than one meaning.** *Hail* can mean ice falling from the sky, or to call out / greet (*hail a taxi*), or to come from (*he hails from Kerala*). *Plague* means a deadly disease, or a large destructive swarm (*a plague of locusts*), or to trouble constantly (*plagued by doubts*).

**Useful phrases from the story (in context):**

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| to be filled with sadness | to feel very sad |
| to start up a correspondence | to begin exchanging letters |
| not the slightest surprise | no surprise at all |
| an act of charity | a kind deed to help the needy |
| a bunch of crooks | a group of dishonest people |

**Grammar: reported speech.** Lencho said, "These aren't raindrops, they are new coins." → Lencho said that those weren't raindrops but new coins. (Present → past; *these* → *those*.)

**Grammar: time words.** Fuentes uses many short time markers — *the following Sunday*, *at daybreak*, *an hour later*. These move the story forward quickly; imitate them in your own story writing.

**Figures of speech.** The coins-for-raindrops idea is a **metaphor**: Lencho says the drops *are* coins, not just *like* coins. The salt-white field is a **simile**. 'An ox of a man' is a **metaphor** too. 'Frozen pearls' for hailstones is another metaphor — beautiful for the children, deadly for the crop.

sections.h: Thinking about the text: model answers
sections.md:
**Q. What did Lencho hope for? Why?** He hoped for a good downpour, because his corn was ripe and the bean flowers promised a fine harvest; rain would ensure the crop and income.

**Q. Why did Lencho say the raindrops were like 'new coins'?** Rain meant a rich harvest, which meant money; the big drops were like ten-cent coins and small ones like fives.

**Q. How did the rain change, and what happened to the fields?** A strong wind brought very large hailstones; for an hour the hail fell, destroying the corn and knocking the flowers off the beans. The field looked as if covered with salt.

**Q. Who or what did Lencho have faith in? What did he do?** In God, who sees everything. He wrote a letter to God asking for 100 pesos to resow and survive, and posted it himself.

**Q. Who read the letter, and what did he do?** The postmaster. He laughed, then admired the faith, collected money from his salary, staff and friends, and sent it signed 'God'.

**Q. Was Lencho surprised to find money? What made him angry?** No — his faith was total. He was angry that only 70 pesos came; he believed God could not err, so the post-office staff must have stolen 30.

**Q. Are there people like Lencho in the real world? (Long answer)** Yes — people with simple, total faith exist in every village and city. Such faith can give great strength in hard times, but it can also blind a person to the human kindness around them. The postmaster represents people who quietly help others. A balanced reader learns from both: keep faith, but also recognise and thank the people through whom help comes.

**Speaking/Writing tasks suggested:** a class discussion on *Is it right to help someone without telling them?*, and a letter from Lencho to the postmaster written after he learns the truth.

story.title: A Letter at Our Dak Ghar (an Indian echo)

parts.md: In a hill village near Almora, a sudden hailstorm in April flattened Ramesh-ji's wheat in twenty minutes. That night his daughter Meena, in Class 10, heard him whisper a prayer by the lamp. The next morning she watched him write a postcard in slow Devanagari: *Bhagwan, beej ke liye paise chahiye.* He addressed it to the temple deity and posted it at the little dak ghar.

The branch postmaster, Joshi-ji, read the card twice. He thought of his own father, a farmer too. He passed a tin box around the bus stand, the tea stall and the school staff room. In a week there was enough for seed. He sent it by money order, signed only 'Ishwar'. Meena later found out the truth and told her father. Ramesh-ji was silent for a long time, then walked to the post office with a basket of apricots. *God answered,* he said, *but He used your hands.* Unlike Lencho, he learned whom to thank — which is exactly the lesson Fuentes leaves for us to discover.

summary: Author: G. L. Fuentes (Gregorio López y Fuentes), Mexican writer of rural life.
Lencho, a farmer, lives in the only house on a hill and hopes for rain for his ripe corn.
He calls the raindrops 'new coins' — rain means money to a farmer.
Rain turns to a fierce hailstorm that destroys the entire crop; the field looks covered with salt.
With faith in God, Lencho writes a letter to God asking for 100 pesos.
The postmaster laughs, then admires the faith and decides to answer it.
He gives part of his salary and collects money from staff and friends — a little more than half.
He signs the reply 'God' to protect Lencho's faith.
Lencho is not surprised by the money but is angry that it is less (70 pesos, so 30 'missing').
His second letter asks God not to use the post, calling the employees 'a bunch of crooks'.
Central irony: the helpers are accused of theft.
Themes: faith, humanity/charity, irony, nature's power over farmers.
Language: words with many meanings (hail, plague), reported speech, simile and metaphor.

rd-school-c10-english-a.ff-madam-rides-b.title: Madam Rides the Bus — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-a.ff-madam-rides-b.subtitle: An eight-year-old saves sixty paise, boards a bus alone, sees the world — and meets death on the road

sections.md:
Have you ever made a secret plan as a child — saving coins in a tin, working out every detail, telling no one? **Valliammai**, called **Valli**, is eight years old. She lives in a village in Tamil Nadu. Every day she stands at the front doorway of her house and watches the street, and the most fascinating thing she sees is the **bus** that travels between her village and the nearest town. It passes through her street **every hour**, once going to the town and once coming back.

The sight of the bus, filled with new passengers each time, is a source of endless joy for her. Day after day she watches it, and a tiny wish grows into a burning ambition: **to ride on that bus**, even once.

*Madam Rides the Bus* is by **Vallikkannan** (pen name of R. S. Krishnaswamy, 1920–2006), a well-known Tamil writer and Sahitya Akademi Award winner; the textbook gives it in English translation. Because it is a recent, copyrighted work, this companion retells it scene by scene in our own words — read the exact text in the free NCERT PDF linked at the end.

The story is a gentle **coming-of-age** tale: a child's first journey into the wider world, and her first meeting with the idea of death.

check.q: What was Valli's 'burning desire'?
options: To go to school in town
check.why: Watching the bus every day from her doorway, Valli longed to ride it at least once.

sections.h: Valli's world: the doorway and the street
sections.md:
Before the plan, the writer shows us how Valli spends her days. Children her age play with friends, but Valli's **favourite pastime** is standing in the front doorway, watching what happens in the street outside. There are no friends of her own age on her street, so the street itself becomes her entertainment — carts, people, animals, and above all, the bus.

This small detail matters. It shows that Valli is **observant** and **curious**. She is a watcher of the world, and watching is no longer enough: she wants to be *inside* the picture. Many readers remember feeling the same about a train, an aeroplane or a city they could only see from a distance.

The bus is also a symbol. For a village child, it is a moving window to the **outside world** — the town, with its shops and crowds, which she has never seen alone.

check.q: Why did Valli spend her time watching the street?
options: She had no playmates of her age on the street and found the street fascinating
She was waiting for her father
check.why: With no friends of her own age nearby, the busy street — especially the bus — became her favourite entertainment.

sections.h: The plan: sixty paise and careful questions
sections.md:
Valli is a planner. She listens carefully to conversations between her neighbours and people who regularly use the bus, and asks a few discreet questions. She learns:

- the town is **six miles** from her village;
- the fare is **thirty paise one way** — so **sixty paise** for a round trip;
- the trip takes **forty-five minutes** each way.

She works out the plan: if she leaves home at **1 p.m.** — when her mother takes her afternoon nap — she can reach the town at 1:45, stay on the bus, and return by **2:45 p.m.**, before her mother wakes. (She does not plan to get off in town; she just wants the ride.)

To get the money, she makes **sacrifices**. She saves every coin that comes her way, **resisting every temptation** — peppermints, toys, balloons, and even a ride on the merry-go-round at the village fair. That last one was particularly hard!

This tells us much about Valli: she is **determined, patient, intelligent and self-controlled** far beyond her years.

check.q: How much money did Valli need for the round trip?
check.why: The fare was thirty paise each way, so a trip to town and back cost sixty paise.

sections.md:
**Scene — the bus stop.** The day comes. At one o'clock, her mother goes to sleep. Valli slips out of the house, walks to the bus stop, and waits. When the bus arrives, she waves it to a stop. The **conductor** jokingly calls out for the passenger — and, seeing a tiny girl, teases that *madam* wants to board.

Valli answers with dignity that she *is* coming, and pays her fare. When the conductor offers to help her climb up, she tells him she can manage alone — she doesn't need anyone to pull her in. He is amused and keeps calling her **madam** — hence the title.

**Scene — inside the bus.** She refuses to be treated as a child. An elderly woman on the bus asks where she is going all alone. Valli finds her nosy. She notices the woman's ugly earrings in big, stretched earlobe holes and her betel-stained mouth, and decides she will not make friends with her. She replies firmly that she can look after herself.

She gets up on the seat to see out of the window. When the conductor warns that she may lose her seat or fall, she replies sharply that she is not a child. The conductor laughs and plays along, treating her as a grown-up lady.

This section is full of **gentle humour**. The adults find Valli charming; Valli takes herself very seriously. Her pride and independence are both funny and admirable.

check.q: Why does the conductor call Valli 'madam'?
options: He was teasing her for behaving like a grown-up
check.why: Valli insisted on behaving like an adult, so the conductor playfully addressed her as 'madam'.

sections.md:
**Scene — the road.** Through the window, Valli sees a whole new world. The bus travels along the bank of a **canal**. On one side are palm trees, grasslands, distant mountains and the deep blue sky. On the other side is a deep ditch and beyond it acres and acres of green fields — green everywhere, as far as her eyes can see.

She is thrilled. Then the bus has to slow suddenly: a young **cow**, tail high in the air, is running right in the middle of the road, just in front of the bus. The driver honks; the frightened cow runs faster and faster. Valli laughs until there are tears in her eyes.

**Scene — the town.** The bus reaches the town bus station and stops. Valli does not get off. She looks out at the shops, the crowds and the colourful things. The conductor asks if she wants to get down and have a drink. She says no. He offers to buy her a cool drink — she again refuses, with dignity, saying she has no money for it and won't take a treat. Her self-respect is strong. She pays thirty paise again and stays in her seat for the return trip.

check.q: Why did Valli refuse the conductor's offer of a cold drink?
options: She had no money and did not want to accept a treat — self-respect
check.why: Valli valued her independence and would not accept something she could not pay for herself.

sections.md:
On the way back, Valli is still watching. And then she sees something by the roadside: the **same young cow** that had made her laugh, now **lying dead** beside the road, killed by some passing vehicle.

The sight shocks her deeply. The happy, lively creature she had laughed at less than an hour ago is now lifeless. Her joy is gone. For the rest of the journey she stays glued to her seat. She no longer wants to look out of the window. The image of the dead cow keeps coming back to her.

This is the **turning point** of the story. Valli, the brave, proud child who wanted to experience everything, comes face to face with **death** for the first time. It is an introduction to a truth of life: things that are alive and joyful can suddenly end. She grows up a little in that moment.

Notice that the author does not explain her feelings in long sentences; he shows us through her behaviour — she no longer wants to look out. This is the art of **showing, not telling**.

**Structure note:** the cow appears twice — alive and funny on the outward trip, dead on the return. This **contrast** (a mirror structure) turns a simple bus ride into a lesson about life and death.
keyTerms: haunt — to keep coming back to someone's mind
turning point — moment of important change in a story
contrast — placing opposites side by side for effect

check.q: Why did Valli lose interest in the view on the way back?
options: She saw the young cow lying dead on the road
check.why: Seeing the same cheerful cow now dead shocked her and took away all her pleasure in the journey.

sections.md:
The bus reaches her village at **2:45 p.m.**, exactly as planned. Valli gets down and says goodbye to the conductor, who cheerfully invites *madam* to ride again. She goes home. Her mother has just woken up and is chatting with Valli's aunt.

The adults talk about things one cannot really know without seeing them for oneself — and Valli, smiling inwardly, makes a mysterious remark of her own. Her mother and aunt do not understand what she means, and she does not explain. Her adventure stays her secret.

**Why the ending works:** the grown-ups think they know everything about the little girl, but she now carries an experience — joy, independence and the shock of death — that they know nothing about. The reader shares the secret with her.

**Why the title works:** *Madam Rides the Bus* captures both the humour (a tiny girl called 'madam') and the achievement (she actually rides the bus alone). It also hints at her dignity — she wants to be treated as a grown-up, and in a way, the trip makes her one.

check.q: What does Valli do about her trip when she reaches home?
check.why: Valli reaches home before her mother notices and keeps her adventure to herself, speaking only in hints.

sections.md:
**Valli** — curious, observant, determined, independent, proud, sensitive. She plans like an adult, saves like an adult and insists on paying her own way, yet she laughs like a child at the running cow and is shaken like a child by its death. She moves from childish joy to a deeper awareness.

**The conductor** — jolly, teasing, kind. He respects her independence, offers her a drink, and treats her game of being grown-up with good humour.

**The elderly woman** — curious and a little nosy; she represents adults who treat children as helpless. Valli's reaction to her (noticing her ugly earrings and refusing to chat) is a little rude but very childlike.

**Valli's mother and aunt** — they appear briefly at the end and remain unaware of the adventure.

**Themes:**
1. **Childhood curiosity** — the urge to see the world beyond the doorway.
2. **Independence and self-respect** — saving her own money, refusing help and treats.
3. **First awareness of death** — life's joy and fragility side by side.
4. **The child's world vs the adult world** — the adults never learn what she has seen.
5. **Growing up** — one afternoon changes her.

**A note for today's readers:** Valli's secret trip makes a good story, but in real life children should always tell a trusted adult before travelling. The story values her courage and planning, not slipping away unsupervised.

**1. Words for feelings.** The story moves through many emotions. Learn to name them: *curious, eager, excited, thrilled, proud, annoyed (with the old woman), amused, shocked, sad, thoughtful*. A common exercise asks you to find words that show Valli's feelings at different points — use this list.

**2. Phrases and their meanings:**

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| a burning desire | a very strong wish |
| to resist temptation | to stop yourself from doing something tempting |
| glued to one's seat | not moving at all |
| to have a good laugh | to laugh heartily |
| as far as the eye could see | to the horizon |

**3. Reported speech.** The conductor asked Valli if she wanted to get down and have a drink. Valli replied that she had no money for it. (Questions become *if/whether*; tenses shift back.)

**4. Showing character through dialogue.** Valli's short, firm replies (*I'm not a child*) reveal pride; the conductor's playful lines reveal good humour. When you write a story, let characters' words show who they are.

**5. Time and sequence words.** *At one o'clock, after forty-five minutes, on the way back, at 2:45* — the story keeps a precise clock, matching Valli's careful planning.

check.q: 'She was glued to her seat' means she…
check.why: To be glued to one's seat is an idiom meaning to stay still and not move, here because she was shocked.

sections.md:
**Q. How did Valli save money for the journey?** She saved every coin she got and resisted every temptation — peppermints, toys, balloons and even a ride on the merry-go-round at the fair — until she had sixty paise.

**Q. Why didn't Valli want to make friends with the elderly woman?** The woman was nosy and treated her as a child; Valli also disliked her ugly earrings and betel-stained mouth, so she answered curtly.

**Q. Why didn't Valli get off the bus at the town?** She had only enough money for the return fare and had planned just the ride; she also wanted to be back before her mother woke at 2:45.

**Q. 'Valli is a grown-up in some ways.' Discuss (120 words).** Valli plans like an adult: she gathers facts discreetly, calculates fare and time, and chooses the hour when her mother sleeps. She saves sixty paise by giving up every childish treat. On the bus she pays her own fare, refuses help climbing in, refuses a free drink out of self-respect, and handles the conductor's teasing with dignity. Yet she is still a child: she stands on the seat, laughs till she cries at a running cow, and is deeply shaken when she sees it dead. The story shows a child on the edge of growing up — and the trip, especially the sight of death, moves her a step forward.

**Q. What does the dead cow mean in the story?** It is Valli's first encounter with death; it shows that life's joys are fragile and marks her move from innocence to awareness.

parts.md: Meera, nine, lived in a Bengaluru suburb and had watched the purple Metro glide past her balcony for a year. For three months she saved coins from her birthday and from helping her grandmother sort coriander. One Saturday, with her mother's permission (and her older cousin two seats away — because times have changed since Valli's), she tapped the token at the gate all by herself and felt a little like a queen.

From the window she saw lakes, a cricket ground, a building site with yellow cranes. Then, near one station, she saw a stray dog limping after being hit by a scooter. A volunteer was already lifting it gently onto a cloth. Meera was quiet the whole way back. At home she told her mother, 'The city is big. Some parts are happy and some are sad.' Her mother nodded; she had read *Madam Rides the Bus* in school too. Growing up, she thought, is seeing both.

summary: Author: Vallikkannan, Tamil writer; story set in a Tamil Nadu village.
Valli (Valliammai), aged eight, watches the hourly bus from her doorway and longs to ride it.
She has no playmates on her street; watching the street is her favourite pastime.
She gathers information discreetly: 6 miles to town, 30 paise each way, 45 minutes.
She saves 60 paise by resisting peppermints, toys, balloons and the merry-go-round.
She leaves at 1 p.m. while her mother naps; plans to be back by 2:45.
The conductor jokingly calls her 'madam'; she insists she is not a child.
She dislikes a nosy elderly woman and refuses to talk to her.
She enjoys the canal, palm trees, mountains, green fields; laughs at a young cow running ahead of the bus.
In town she does not get off and refuses a free cold drink — self-respect.
On return, she sees the same cow lying dead; her joy vanishes.
She reaches home in time and keeps the adventure secret.
Themes: curiosity, independence, first awareness of death, growing up.

rd-school-c10-english-a.ff-mijbil-otter.title: Mijbil the Otter — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-a.ff-mijbil-otter.subtitle: A writer, a playful otter from the Iraqi marshes, a bathtub, a train journey and one very surprised airline

sections.h: A hook: what would you do with a pet otter?
sections.md:
Imagine bringing home a pet that turns your bathtub into a swimming pool, juggles marbles on its belly, and sulks if you leave it alone. Now imagine trying to take it on a plane.

That is the story of **Mijbil the Otter**, adapted from the book *Ring of Bright Water* (1960) by the Scottish naturalist and writer **Gavin Maxwell** (1914–1969). Maxwell was travelling in the marshes of southern **Iraq** in **1956**. His dog had died, and he felt lonely. During the journey he decided he would like to keep an otter instead — the Tigris marshes were full of them, and his travelling companion encouraged the idea.

The chapter is funny, affectionate and full of close observation. It is also a study of how a human and an animal slowly learn to trust each other.

Maxwell died in 1969, so the book is still in copyright: this companion retells every scene in our own words and explains it — read the exact text in the free NCERT PDF linked at the end.

> Did you know? The otter Maxwell kept turned out to be a sub-species unknown to science at the time. It was named **Maxwell's otter** (*Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli*) after him — a variety of the smooth-coated otter, which is also found in India.
keyTerms: otter — a water-loving mammal with webbed feet, related to weasels
marshes — wet, swampy land
naturalist — expert who studies animals and plants

sections.h: Before you read: meet the otter
sections.md:
The textbook's pre-reading activity asks you to look at a picture of an otter and guess what kind of animal it is — a useful warm-up, because the whole comedy of the London section depends on people *not* knowing.

| Feature | Otter facts |
|---|---|
| Family | weasels (mustelids) — cousins of badgers and minks |
| Body | long, slim, with a strong flat tail for steering |
| Feet | webbed, good for swimming; front paws can hold and juggle objects |
| Fur | very dense and waterproof; Mij's was dark brown and velvety |
| Food | mainly fish, also frogs, crabs, insects |
| Nature | playful, intelligent, social; love to slide, roll and splash |
| In India | smooth-coated, small-clawed and Eurasian otters live in rivers and wetlands |

Keep these facts in mind: almost every funny scene in the chapter grows out of a real otter behaviour.

sections.h: Getting Mijbil: Basra and a sack
sections.md:
**Scene 1 — waiting in Basra.** Maxwell travels to **Basra**, to the **Consulate-General**, to collect and answer mail from Europe. His mail hasn't arrived. He waits; when he telephones and cables, he learns it is on the way. Meanwhile his friend, who was to accompany him, goes on ahead.

**Scene 2 — the sack.** One evening, Maxwell returns to his bedroom to find two **Arabs** squatting on the floor with a **sack** that is wriggling. It contains a male otter, along with a note from his friend that amounts to: *here is your otter*. With the opening of that sack, Maxwell writes (in effect), began a phase of his life that has not ended yet.

**Mijbil's look.** The otter is very small, slender, rather like a tiny dragon from a medieval drawing. From head to tail he is coated with pointed scales of dried mud, between which the tips of velvet fur can be glimpsed. Once the mud is washed off, he is revealed as a small creature with dark chocolate-brown fur, soft as velvet.

**The name.** Maxwell calls him **Mijbil**, after a sheikh he and his friend had stayed with, and for short, **Mij**.

**The first day.** For the first 24 hours, Mijbil is neither hostile nor friendly; he is simply **aloof and indifferent**, choosing to sleep on the floor as far from the bed as possible. But on the second night he comes onto the bed and sleeps in the crook of Maxwell's knees until the servant brings tea in the morning. From then on, he begins to trust.

check.q: How did Mijbil behave during his first twenty-four hours with Maxwell?
check.why: For the first day Mijbil kept his distance, neither hostile nor friendly, sleeping far from Maxwell's bed.

sections.md:
**Scene 3.** On the second day, Mijbil becomes interested in his surroundings. Maxwell takes him to the bathroom on a leash. For half an hour, Mij goes **wild with joy** in the water — plunging, rolling, shooting up and down the length of the bathtub, making enough slosh and splash for a hippo.

Maxwell notices that this is a characteristic of otters: **every drop of water must be spread around**. A bowl must be overturned or, if it won't overturn, be sat in and sloshed in until it overflows. Water must be kept on the move and made to do things; still water seems to them wasted and annoying.

A little later, Mij escapes from the bedroom and is found in the bathroom, struggling with the **tap**. In a short time he learned to turn it on all by himself.

**The leash.** At first, Maxwell takes Mij on a leash to the bathroom. Soon Mij learns to follow without one, and to come when called. He adores the water so much that the bath becomes his playground.

**Observation tip for exams:** Maxwell's writing is precise and scientific but also playful. He gives exact behaviours (turning the tap, spreading water) and compares them humorously (a hippo's splashing).

check.q: What did Maxwell observe about otters and water?
options: Water must be spread around and kept moving
check.why: Maxwell noticed that otters love to splash and spill water; for them, still water is wasted and must be made to move.

sections.md:
**Scene 4.** Mij spends hours **playing**. His favourite toys are **marbles**. He lies on his back and juggles them on his broad, webbed paws, sometimes keeping two on his stomach without ever dropping one.

His other favourite is a **rubber ball**, which he pushes around the room, and a **game of his own** with a suitcase. One of Maxwell's suitcases lay at a slight slope; Mij discovered that if he placed a ball at the top, it would roll down. He would rush round to the other end to receive it, then go back and do it again — a game he invented entirely by himself, evidence of intelligence and fun.

Otters, Maxwell notes, are not like dogs. A dog is obedient; an otter wants to be with you, but on its own terms. When Mij is left alone, he **sulks**. When Maxwell returns, he greets him warmly.

**Language note:** Maxwell's verbs are lively: *juggle, plunge, wriggle, sulk, scamper*. Use them in your descriptive writing.

check.q: Which game did Mij invent on his own?
options: Rolling a ball down a sloping suitcase and catching it at the other end
check.why: Mij discovered the suitcase slope and repeatedly rolled a ball down it, running to catch it — a self-made game.

sections.h: The journey to London: a crisis in a box
sections.md:
**Scene 5 — the rules.** Maxwell must fly back to **London** with Mij. The British airline flying direct would not carry animals, so he books a flight to **Paris** with a connection to London. The airline insists that Mij be packed in a **box** not more than **18 inches square**, to be placed on the floor at Maxwell's feet.

**Scene 6 — the bloody box.** An hour before leaving for the airport, Maxwell puts Mij into the box and goes to eat a hurried meal. When he returns, there is **silence** from the box — and blood around the air-holes. Mij has torn the lining to shreds trying to escape, and has cut his mouth and paws. Time is very short.

Maxwell, in a panic, rips out the remaining lining, puts Mij back in the box and rushes to the airport, holding it shut.

**Scene 7 — chaos on the plane.** On board, he has been given a seat at the front; a kind **air hostess** suggests he keep Mij on his knees. Maxwell unfastens the box — and Mij escapes! He disappears at high speed down the aisle. There are shrieks; a woman stands on her seat screaming that there is a rat. Maxwell crawls under seats trying to catch him, ending up with his face smeared in curry from a passenger's plate. Finally the air hostess helps, and Mij is returned to Maxwell, who holds him on his knee for the rest of the flight. Mij nuzzles his face, and peace returns.
